messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] proposal draft for RStan interface
messages.body_plain:
So my big problem with this flat structure is a conceptual one.
Right now there’s a glut of terrible algorithm names out there
because people don’t understand the foundations of HMC.
Consequently "Hamiltonian Monte Carlo” is often relegated
to what is more properly called Metropolis-Corrected Euclidean
Hamiltonian Monte Carlo with a static integration time, and
every tweak yields a new name.  This flurry of names obfuscates
the real underlying mathematical framework — changing the
metric doesn’t really lead to a new algorithm, just a different
implementation.  Why, for example, would RHMC receive
its own command but EHMC with a diagonal metric vs EHMC
with a dense metric would be different options within the same
command?  Moreover, a single command “stan_hmc” that
just calls one of this configurations makes everything so much
worse.

At the very least we need to be more careful with the names.
I know we all love NUTS, but it’s really just an implementation
of a more general idea of dynamic integration time (really the
no-U-turn part of it is the least novel — the really important
part of the algorithm is binary tree to preserve reversibility).
What we have are two main different configuration options:

Metric: Identity, diagonal Euclidean, dense Euclidean (and in the future SoftAbs Riemannian)
Integration Time: Static vs Exhaustive (i.e. integrate longer on bigger level sets, NUTS is an example)

Why is integration time a better split than metric?

Then there’s the fact that we can sample or optimize, and
the current names make no distinction between the two
If people are that against hierarchical arguments (note
that we have yet to have any complaint from users on
the list — the CmdStan user base is small, but it’s not
negligible) then we  at least have to maintain the hierarchy
is the command names: stan_mcmc_*, stan_opt_*, stan_vb_*, etc.

Finally, maintaining this orgy of commands is going to be a
pain in the ass.  What to change one argument that all of the
commands share?  Go ahead and tweak every single command
config.

On May 21, 2015, at 11:05 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> Ahead of working on the Python/R under-the-hood refactor when
> Allen gets here, I tried to go through the current R interface and
> whittle things down (and expand a bit) to where I think it should go.
> I'd think that roughly the same interface would work in Python.
>
> I hope this is close enough to idiomatic for R that it's not
> too embarrassing --- but please send feedback (up to and including
> telling me I should just stay out of R!).
>
> The biggest change is simplifying what functions do and where some
> of the action is, as well as splitting some of the functions out (like
> stan() is now stan_nuts, stan_hmc, and stan_diagnose).
>
> I don't think this loses any functionality other than the big fit
> object, which I don't think we should have.  And it's assuming some
> functionality we don't yet have, like being able to input a mass matrix.
>
> I can move this over to a wiki (on RStan or Stan's repo?) if people
> think that'll be easier and the response isn't to just get out of the
> way of RStan.
>
> - Bob
>
>
> 1.  Compilation
> ------------------------------------------------------------
> The compilation function compiles a Stan program to a dynamic shared
> object (DSO) and optionally saves it.
>
> compiled_program
> rtan::stan_compile(                # DEFAULTS
>  source = (<string> || <path>)    # no default
>  name = <string>,                 # empty
>  boost = <path>,                  # use BH
>  eigen = <path>,                  # use RcppEigen
>  opt = ("fast" || "debug"),       # "fast"
>  save_dso = <bool>,               # FALSE
>  debug_code = <bool>              # TRUE
> );
>
> * Is there any reason to keep the name option?
> * How long-lived is the "save_dso" option?
>    - Where is it saved?
> * If we allow optimize settings, is there a way to have it scope
>  over just the call and not affect the R global build environment?
> * Is there a way we can have make-like behavior here where if there's
>  a saved version and the model file or code have not changed, don't
>  do anything?
> * Do we need the other existing compiler options ("presentation1",
>  "presentation2", and "small")?
> * Should the save_dso provide a path rather than a boolean?
> * Is it possible to save the DSO across sessions?
> * Should the dave_dso defalt be true and if so, use temp?
> * Do we ever need NDEBUG=false?  That is, shouldn't we just always
>  have -DNDEBUG set to turn off debugging?  (The double-negative
>
> compiled_program
> --------------------
> This should only include the compiled Stan program and methods
> to do variable conversion, extract names, compute log densities, etc.
>
> Slots:
>  name : <string>
>  stan_code : <string>
>  cpp_code  : <string>
>  dso : <S4 cxxdso>  (from inline)
>  cxx_flags: <string>
> Methods:
>  double
>  log_prob(
>    unconstrained_params = <vector>,
>    jacobian = <bool>);
>
>  list(value=<double>, grad=<vector>)
>  log_prob_grad(
>    unconstrained_params = <vector>,
>    jacobian = <bool>);
>
>      return$value : <double>
>      return$grad : <vector>
>
>  list(
>  constrain_params(
>    unconstrained_params = <vector>);
>
>  vector
>  constrain_params_vec(
>    unconstrained_params = <vector>);
>
>  vector
>  unconstrain_params(
>    params = (<list> || vector));
>
> * Seems there should be a better way to organize this, but I
>  can't see it.  And maybe some shorter names
>
>
> 2. NUTS
> ------------------------------------------------------------
>
> mcmc_fit
> rstan::stan_nuts(
>  program = <compiled_program>,       # no default
>  data = (<list> || <environment>),   # top-level environment by default
>  max_treedepth = <int>,              # 10
>  chain_ids = <ints>,                 # 1:4
>  num_warmup = <int>,                 # 10
>  num_samples = <int>,                # 10
>  init=(<double>                      # 2.0
>        || <list>
>        || <list of lists>
>        || <function>)
>  stepsize=<double>,                  # 1.0
>  metric = ("unit_e",                 # "diag_e"
>           || "diag_e"
>           || "dense_e"
>           || <vector>
>           || <matrix>),
>  adapt_stepsize = <bool>,            # TRUE
>  adapt_mass_matrix = <bool>,         # TRUE
>  adapt = list(gamma=<double>,
>               kappa=<double>,
>               t0=<double>,
>               init_buffer=<int>,
>               term_buffer=<int>,
>               adapt_window=<int>)    # ...
>  params_to_save = (NA
>                   || <vector(char)>) # NA
>  save_warmup = <bool>,               # TRUE
>  thin = <int>,                       # 1
>  sample_file = <path>,               # NA
>  diagnostic_file = <path>,           # NA
>  refresh = <int>,                    # 1
>  verbose = ("quiet"
>             || "standard"
>             || "verbose"),           # standard
>  seed = <int>                        # random from R
> )
>
> * Return value just includes the result in such a way that it
>  can be extracted as before.
> * Return value won't include the compiled program (or source).
> * Should return value include timing information?
> * There's no append_samples = <bool>
> * There's no option to compile the model from within the stan_nuts
>  call.
> * data defaults to top-level environment with lazy read (not how
>  it's done now);  list is list of values as before
> * Instead of "chains" and a start ID, there's just a "chain_ids"
>  argument supplying both the chains and the ID, defaulting to the usual
> * Default num_warmup and num_samples very small by default (but shouldn't
>  be so small as to trigger scary messages about adaptation)
> * Metric is specified by name of type or by value;  the names default
>  to unit values for init
> * Those adapt parameters are all for adapt_stepsize, right?
> * Are there adaptation parameters for mass_matrix, like regularization?
> * params_to_save defaults to NA (or all), or a positive list of whole
>  parameter names.
> * sample_file gets a copy of the output written to it, but return
>  object still created --- should this just move so that the return
>  object has a save on it?  Or should setting this cause the return of
>  this function to be NA?
>
> mcmc_fit
> --------------------
>
>
> 3. EHMC
> ------------------------------------------------------------
> Plain old HMC looks just like NUTS, but with max_treedepth replaced
> by integration time:
>
> mcmc_fit
> rstan::stan_hmc(...
>  int_time = <double>
>  ...
> )
>
>
> 4. Optimize
> ------------------------------------------------------------
>
> optimization_fit
> stan_lbfgs(
>  program = <compiled_program>,
>  data = (<list> || <environment>),
>  init = (<double>
>          || <list>
>          || <list of lists>
>          || <function>),
>  optimization_file = <file>,
>  verbose = ("quiet" || "verbose"),
>  hessian = <bool>,                       # FALSE
>  max_iterations = <int>,                 # NA
>  save_iterations = <bool>,               # FALSE
>  refresh = <int>,                        # 5
>  init_alpha = <double>,                  # ???
>  tol_obj = <double>,
>  tol_grad = <double>,
>  tol_param = <double>,
>  tol_obj_rel = <double>,
>  tol_grad_rel = <double>,
>  tol_param_rel = <double>,
>  seed = <int>
> )
>
>
> * Should verbose be a boolean?
> * What does current as_vector do? Current doc says "flag indicating whether a
>  vector is used to for the point estimate found. A list can be
>  used instead by specifying it to be FALSE"
> * What's the behavior of tolerances if more than one's specified?  I'd
>  think it should be read as AND or as OR.
> * No option to specify parameter return as vector --- use a compiled
>  model's conversion.
>
> optimization_fit
> --------------------
>    $par : parameters (as list)
>    $value : lp__
>
>
> 5. Diagnose
> ------------------------------------------------------------
>
> diagnostics
> rstan::stan_diagnose(
>  program = <compiled_program>,
>  data = (<list> || <environment>),
>  init = (<double>
>          || <list>
>          || <list of lists>
>          || <function>),
>  epsilon = <double>,
>  error_threshold = <double>,
>  seed = <int>,
>  chain_ids = <int>)
>
> * arguments just a subset of those for NUTS/HMC
> * returns diagnostics for each of the chain_ids
> * not sure what goes in diagnostics as long as it's
>  easy to print
>
> diagnostics
> --------------------
> ?? not sure what should go in here --- it needs to be printable
>
> ==============================================================================
>

I agree that maintaining this multitude of commands is going to be a
pain in the ass. I think it will be *slightly* easier than the status
quo, which requires a giant switch statement depending on the algorithm
to do the same thing.

More concretely: I've been bitten once by a typo in handling/"parsing"
the unwieldy config object (same config object in RStan and PyStan) and
I think using functions would make those kinds of errors much easier to
spot.

Bref, I don't see how it will make things worse and it might make things
better.

Thanks,

Allen

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] proposal draft for RStan interface
messages.body_plain:
I have sympathy --- my problem with the hiearchical structure
is a conceptual one, too.

There are two things I'm suggesting doing differently:

  * flattening arguments
  * separating top-level commands

My main motivation is to simplify the functions from
the user's perspective by removing argument interactions and
making the functions or command-line invocations more idiomatic.
And also make backward compatibility easier.

So the reason plain-old Euclidean HMC is split from
NUTS is that they take two conflicting config params
(integration time and max depth; whereas the metric is just
a free choice).

The downside is that it increases the number of functions.
This would be bad if a lot of them were used and you had
to constantly choose which one to use.

I can live with stan_mcmc_...  and stan_opt_...

I think the full set of top-level commands now would be:

 SHORT               LONG

 stan_lbfgs          stan_opt_lbfgs
 stan_bfgs           stan_opt_bfgs

 stan_hmc            stan_mcmc_hmc_static
 stan_nuts           stan_mcmc_hmc_nuts

 stan_diagnose       stan_diagnose

I think the following are in our short-term future:

 stan_bbvb           stan_approx_bbvb

 stan_rhmc           stan_mcmc_hmc_static_riemannian
 stan_geonuts        stan_mcmc_hmc_nuts_riemannian

and maybe

 stan_stochastic_bbvb      stan_approx_stochastic_bbvb

 stan_mml                  stan_opt_mml

I'm particularly worried about backward compatibility in
the hierarchical formulation.

I think Andrew/Ben/Rob want to include something to parse
the lme4/glm syntax to implement somehting like:

 stan_glm                   ???
 stan_lme                   ???

- Bob

be used for any command.  It’s too general and will
confound the already bad naming conventions in the
literature.  Especially when it’s compared to “stan_nuts”
which is not a proper dichotomy.

The more appropriate names would be

stan_mcmc_ehmc_static
stan_mcmc_ehmc_exhaustive

which would then generalize to

stan_mcmc_rhmc_static
stan_mcmc_rhmc_exhaustive

Short names don’t help — if we want a default that
users can call without knowing what they’re doing
then we should just have a “stan_sample” method
that defaults to out current favorite method.

As for glm and lme should these be model format
options?  As in you can input a model in the Stan
modeling language, or the glm language, or the
lme language.

messages.body_plain:
> On Jun 1, 2015, at 4:06 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> No, no, no, no, no, no.  At no point should “stan_hmc”
> be used for any command.  It’s too general and will
> confound the already bad naming conventions in the
> literature.  Especially when it’s compared to “stan_nuts”
> which is not a proper dichotomy.
>
> The more appropriate names would be
>
> stan_mcmc_ehmc_static

I think the "e" and "static" are defaults and "mcmc" is implied by "hmc",
so it's back to my preferred command,

  stan_hmc

by the usual function naming principles (where we treat the noun
"hmc" as an infinitive verb,  as in "to verb a noun").

> stan_mcmc_ehmc_exhaustive

Why "exhaustive" for NUTS?

Language is just messy, though we can control these usages if you
really think it's necessary (I don't here and think the longer names
will just be more confusing).

It's completely typical to have a generic term that's also used
for a specific instance.  For instance, "blue" might be either a cover
or a contrast to "sky blue" and "navy blue".

And you don't see commands in languages like R that say things like:

  mypackagename_linear_regression_nonheteroscedastic_normal_noise(...)

you see commands like lm(), where the lack of "g" means it's plain
old linear regression and the normal noise is taken for granted.

> which would then generalize to
>
> stan_mcmc_rhmc_static
> stan_mcmc_rhmc_exhaustive
>
> Short names don’t help — if we want a default that
> users can call without knowing what they’re doing
> then we should just have a “stan_sample” method
> that defaults to out current favorite method.
>
> As for glm and lme should these be model format
> options?  As in you can input a model in the Stan
> modeling language, or the glm language, or the
> lme language.

You'll have to ask Andrew et al.  I think the goal was
to have a drop-in replacement for R's glm(), which would
be different than a model-specification option for a
Stan call.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] proposal draft for RStan interface
messages.body_plain:
> I think the "e" and "static" are defaults and "mcmc" is implied by "hmc",
> so it's back to my preferred command,
>
>  stan_hmc

I am warning everyone that I will fight this hard.  If we want to
abstract to a default then just go with stan_sample or stan_mcmc.
stan_hmc just reinforces this false idea that people have that
HMC is just Euclidean HMC with a static integration time and
every other config is some fancy new algorithm.  But it’s not —
HMC is a very general construction and we need to emphasize
this so that people understand we’re just not offering a new
heuristic algorithm but an entirely new perspective of MCMC.

>> stan_mcmc_ehmc_exhaustive
>
> Why "exhaustive" for NUTS?

It’s what were calling a new class of algorithms with dynamic
integration times (as in the integration time expands until
the trajectory “exhausts” exploration on the level set).  NUTS
is an example — the binary tree to preserve detailed balance
will be a general element of these methods, although the NUTS
criterion itself may likely change to something more theoretically
motivated.

> And you don't see commands in languages like R that say things like:
>
>  mypackagename_linear_regression_nonheteroscedastic_normal_noise(...)
>
> you see commands like lm(), where the lack of "g" means it's plain
> old linear regression and the normal noise is taken for granted.

And people also use “Metropolis” to refer to Random Walk Metropolis
with an isotropic Gaussian proposal, which causes no end of confusion.
For example, I keep hearing “Metropolis is random walk, so all Metropolis
algorithms are bad, right?” which confuses the hell out of people when
you try to respond with HMC being implemented with a Metropolis correction
in practice.  Notation and conventions are terrible in statistical software and
that’s no excuse for us to use poor names, too.

Again, if you want to have a default sampling config fine.  But don’t make
a default HMC config and call it “stan_hmc” or we’ll be digging out of that
convention for a long, long time.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Stiff ode solver
messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob,

There's quite a large collection of possible arguments for CVODE, so I'm struggling to decide what to make available and what to leave as defaults. Also I'm new to CVODE having been a regular LSODA user. Based on an initial read of the CVODE docs I recommend the following as arguments in the "expert" function. I nay suggest more on further reading.

* Arguments of CVodeCreate(lmm, iter)
** lmm = linear multistep method: CV ADAMS or CV BDF
** iter = type of nonlinear solver iteration: CV NEWTON
or CV FUNCTIONAL.
** You could restrict this to the pairs (CV ADAMS, CV FUNCTIONAL) for nonstiff
problems and (CV BDF, CV NEWTON) for stiff problems.

* Linear solver used for Newton iterations: cvdense, cvband, cvklu, cvsuperlumt, cvdiag, cvspgmr, cvspbcg, or cvsptfqmr.
** I could live with the default (CVDENSE), but models involving large systems with specific matrix structures could benefit from the choice.

Cheers,
Bill

messages.body_plain:
On Monday, June 1, 2015 at 8:36:48 PM UTC-4, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Monday, June 1, 2015 at 5:24:26 PM UTC-4, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> > Again, if you want to have a default sampling config fine.  But don’t make
> > a default HMC config and call it “stan_hmc” or we’ll be digging out of that
> > convention for a long, long time.
>
> If we make the various configs into formal classes, we can just have the sampling() (or whatever we rename it to) dispatch on the config object in addition to the model object). Then we wouldn't have a proliferation of function names, just a proliferation of class names for the config objects.

I quickly reimplemented the current configuration as S4 classes in R (attached). After a source(), you could do
new("stan_hmc")
or whatever to instantiate an object that has the defaults for HMC. This retains the hierarchical structure of CmdStan calls, validates the input, doesn't have slots that are inapplicable given other options, and does not require us to write too many functions that are callable by the user. Instead, we can write "methods" for the, e.g., sampling() generic function that dispatch according to the class of the config object.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: proposal draft for RStan interface
messages.body_plain:
Just going through some of the details of this ...

On Thursday, May 21, 2015 at 6:06:47 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> 1.  Compilation
> ------------------------------------------------------------
> The compilation function compiles a Stan program to a dynamic shared
> object (DSO) and optionally saves it.
>
> compiled_program
> rtan::stan_compile(                # DEFAULTS
>   source = (<string> || <path>)    # no default
>   name = <string>,                 # empty
>   boost = <path>,                  # use BH
>   eigen = <path>,                  # use RcppEigen
>   opt = ("fast" || "debug"),       # "fast"
>   save_dso = <bool>,               # FALSE
>   debug_code = <bool>              # TRUE
> );
> * Is there any reason to keep the name option?

I don't think it hurts anything and the name comes up in some of the printed output.

> * How long-lived is the "save_dso" option?
>     - Where is it saved?

It is kind of confusing. The save_dso option currently just makes the dso part of the stanfit object but you have to manually save the stanfit object to the disk to reuse it in a different session. But this is partially obsoleted by the 2.7.0 behavior if the auto_write option is enabled, in which case it is saving the compiled model object to the disk (in the same directory as the .stan file).

> * If we allow optimize settings, is there a way to have it scope
>   over just the call and not affect the R global build environment?

The inline package doesn't permit passing opt and debug_code to CXX. That has to come from a ~./R/Makevars file.

> * Is there a way we can have make-like behavior here where if there's
>   a saved version and the model file or code have not changed, don't
>   do anything?

Already implemented for 2.7.0.

> * Do we need the other existing compiler options ("presentation1",
>   "presentation2", and "small")?

Can't pass them anyway but they were just aliases for -O1, -O2, and -Os.

> * Should the save_dso provide a path rather than a boolean?

No. In 2.7.0, it only looks for a foo.rda file in the same directory as foo.stan.

> * Is it possible to save the DSO across sessions?

Not for the cxxdso object per se but yes for the stanmodel object that has a slot for the cxxdso object.

> * Should the save_dso defalt be true and if so, use temp?

Yes, that is what it does currently. I don't see much reason to ever specify save_dso = FALSE.

> * Do we ever need NDEBUG=false?  That is, shouldn't we just always
>   have -DNDEBUG set to turn off debugging?

Can't pass it, but in the future I would like NDEBUG to turn off some checks. But that is a Stan thing rather than an interface thing.

> compiled_program
> --------------------
> This should only include the compiled Stan program and methods
> to do variable conversion, extract names, compute log densities, etc.

Okay, but this would be backwards uncompatible since log_prob() and stuff are currently defined for stanfit objects because they need the data associated with them. So they are going to have to take data arguments. And we should have log_hessian() and maybe laplace_approximation().

> 2. NUTS
> ------------------------------------------------------------
>
> mcmc_fit
> rstan::stan_nuts(

I disagree with having so many suffixed functions for users. I think we should instead code something like

setMethod("sampling", signature(program = "compiled_program", config = "stan_sample"),
          definition = function(program, config, data, pars, init, ...) {
  # implement
})

where an object of stan_nuts (or stan_fixed or whatever) class could be passed to the config argument or if not, a default one would be instantiated and used.

> * Return value just includes the result in such a way that it
>   can be extracted as before.

OK

> * Return value won't include the compiled program (or source).

I don't see how including the compiled_program would hurt anything

> * Should return value include timing information?

Some people have asked for it, although currdently we don't do so programatically

> * There's no append_samples = <bool>

OK

> * There's no option to compile the model from within the stan_nuts
>   call.

I don't think there should be a stan_nuts() call, but either way, it should pass the compiled_model in.

> * data defaults to top-level environment with lazy read (not how
>   it's done now);  list is list of values as before

I'll implement that for 2.7.0 since no one objected to what I posted before. It is technically the environments in R's lexical order rather than always the top-level environment.

> * Instead of "chains" and a start ID, there's just a "chain_ids"

Currently (and I think it should stay this way in the future) sampling() only does one chain, so it only needs to know the singular chain_id for the chain it is doing. Whatever is driving it whether it is in serial or parallel should be responsible for passing it the seed, chain_id, etc.

> * Default num_warmup and num_samples very small by default (but shouldn't
>   be so small as to trigger scary messages about adaptation)

Are you proposing changing the defaults of num_warmup and num_samples (1000 each)? If so, then we should do that for all the interfaces.

> * Metric is specified by name of type or by value;  the names default
>   to unit values for init
> * Those adapt parameters are all for adapt_stepsize, right?

Yeah, although I think the various configs should have their own class structure.

> * Are there adaptation parameters for mass_matrix, like regularization?

Not currently but we could add them.

> * params_to_save defaults to NA (or all), or a positive list of whole
>   parameter names.

I'm not sure whether it is worth renaming the pars argument params_to_save, in part because in 2.7.0 there is an include = TRUE argument, so you could specify pars = "Sigma", include = FALSE to exclude Sigma but include everything else.

> * sample_file gets a copy of the output written to it, but return
>   object still created --- should this just move so that the return
>   object has a save on it?  Or should setting this cause the return of
>   this function to be NA?

I think it should still return the regular stuff, in addition to writing the sample_file(s).

> mcmc_fit
> --------------------
>
>
> 3. EHMC
> ------------------------------------------------------------
> Plain old HMC looks just like NUTS, but with max_treedepth replaced
> by integration time:

I would say they should be siblings in the class hierarchy for stan_config objects but get called the same way.

> 4. Optimize
> ------------------------------------------------------------
>
> optimization_fit
> stan_lbfgs(

Same deal. I think stan_lbfgs should be a class that inherits from stan_bfgs class with an additional slot for history_size but the user would call something like

stan_optimize(compiled_program, config, data, init, verbose, ...)

> * Should verbose be a boolean?

Yes

> * What does current as_vector do? Current doc says "flag indicating whether a
>   vector is used to for the point estimate found. A list can be
>   used instead by specifying it to be FALSE"

If as_vector = TRUE, then only a vector of optimal parameters is returned. If as_vector = FALSE, then there is more stuff returned with the list.

> * What's the behavior of tolerances if more than one's specified?  I'd
>   think it should be read as AND or as OR.

Don't know.

> * No option to specify parameter return as vector --- use a compiled
>   model's conversion.

But the compiled_model doesn't know what the optimal parameter values are. At least it doesn't currently.

>
> optimization_fit
> --------------------
>     $par : parameters (as list)
>     $value : lp__

And $hessian optionally

> 5. Diagnose
> ------------------------------------------------------------
>
> diagnostics
> rstan::stan_diagnose(

I think stan_diagnose should be a subclass of stan_config with epsilon and error_threshold that can be passed to stan_sample() or stan_optimize() like any other stan_config object.

> diagnostics
> --------------------
> ?? not sure what should go in here --- it needs to be printable

It doesn't exactly print (in the R sense currently) but the gradients get written to R's stream from C++. I don't think the gradients get saved anywhere currently, although we could do that.

Ben

> On Jun 2, 2015, at 12:47 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Just going through some of the details of this ...
>
> On Thursday, May 21, 2015 at 6:06:47 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> 1.  Compilation
> ------------------------------------------------------------
> The compilation function compiles a Stan program to a dynamic shared
> object (DSO) and optionally saves it.
>
> compiled_program
> rtan::stan_compile(                # DEFAULTS
>   source = (<string> || <path>)    # no default
>   name = <string>,                 # empty
>   boost = <path>,                  # use BH
>   eigen = <path>,                  # use RcppEigen
>   opt = ("fast" || "debug"),       # "fast"
>   save_dso = <bool>,               # FALSE
>   debug_code = <bool>              # TRUE
> );
> * Is there any reason to keep the name option?
>
> I don't think it hurts anything and the name comes up in some of the printed output.

What it hurts is readability of the doc and maintainability of
the code.

> * How long-lived is the "save_dso" option?
>     - Where is it saved?
>
> It is kind of confusing. The save_dso option currently just makes the dso part of the stanfit object but you have to manually save the stanfit object to the disk to reuse it in a different session.

I'd like to make the more fine-grained objects available, like
being able to take the DSO and give it new data without recompiling.
(More on this below.)

> But this is partially obsoleted by the 2.7.0 behavior if the auto_write option is enabled, in which case it is saving the compiled model object to the disk (in the same directory as the .stan file).
>
> * If we allow optimize settings, is there a way to have it scope
>   over just the call and not affect the R global build environment?
>
> The inline package doesn't permit passing opt and debug_code to CXX. That has to come from a ~./R/Makevars file.
>
> * Is there a way we can have make-like behavior here where if there's
>   a saved version and the model file or code have not changed, don't
>   do anything?
>
> Already implemented for 2.7.0.

Fantastic.  It's working now?  I thought you'd said it was very fragile.

> * Do we need the other existing compiler options ("presentation1",
>   "presentation2", and "small")?
>
> Can't pass them anyway but they were just aliases for -O1, -O2, and -Os.

What does "can't pass them" mean?  If they're impossible, we should remove
them from the doc.

> * Should the save_dso provide a path rather than a boolean?
>
> No. In 2.7.0, it only looks for a foo.rda file in the same directory as foo.stan.

OK

> * Is it possible to save the DSO across sessions?
>
> Not for the cxxdso object per se but yes for the stanmodel object that has a slot for the cxxdso object.

Would it be possible?  It would be super great if we had
a DSO wrapper object and it was saveable, and an instantiated
object that could be saved.

> * Should the save_dso defalt be true and if so, use temp?
>
> Yes, that is what it does currently. I don't see much reason to ever specify save_dso = FALSE.

OK, then I think we should get rid of the option.

> * Do we ever need NDEBUG=false?  That is, shouldn't we just always
>   have -DNDEBUG set to turn off debugging?
>
> Can't pass it, but in the future I would like NDEBUG to turn off some checks. But that is a Stan thing rather than an interface thing.

Couldn't we do a preliminary call to set_cppo() or the like, or
would that run afoul of CRAN policy on explicitness of side effects?

> compiled_program
> --------------------
> This should only include the compiled Stan program and methods
> to do variable conversion, extract names, compute log densities, etc.
>
> Okay, but this would be backwards uncompatible since log_prob() and stuff are currently defined for stanfit objects because they need the data associated with them. So they are going to have to take data arguments. And we should have log_hessian() and maybe laplace_approximation().

I would very much like to move away from packing so much into
the fit object.   I think we should maintain backward compatibility
until Stan 3, but there's no reason we can't introduce things the way
we want them and mark others as deprecated.

You're right that I missed a level here.

1.  Compiled program --- this is the DSO thing.

2.  Instantiated program class --- this is the program wedded
to its data.

We actually need the instance in (2) to do anything I suggested.

> 2. NUTS
> ------------------------------------------------------------
>
> mcmc_fit
> rstan::stan_nuts(
>
> I disagree with having so many suffixed functions for users. I think we should instead code something like
>
> setMethod("sampling", signature(program = "compiled_program", config = "stan_sample"),
>           definition = function(program, config, data, pars, init, ...) {
>   # implement
> })
>
> where an object of stan_nuts (or stan_fixed or whatever) class could be passed to the config argument or if not, a default one would be instantiated and used.

OK --- Rob unwound what all this meant for me, which I think means
that it'll be used as follows:

  > program <- stan_model(...);
  > fit <- sampling(program, config, ...);

where the config is a required argument to sampling().

Then the idea's to do what Michael likes and have a big config object
that works for everything --- optimization, MCMC, diagnosis, and whatever
else comes up?  Or do you like breaking things out into sampling(),
optimizing(), diagnosing(), vbing() etc.?

I'd want to make things flatter, but I can live with this.

With this, would we need the top-level stan() object to make
people happy (again, I don't want to rip it out ASAP --- not until
an RStan 3 was solidified).

> * Return value just includes the result in such a way that it
>   can be extracted as before.
>
> OK
>
> * Return value won't include the compiled program (or source).
>
> I don't see how including the compiled_program would hurt anything

It makes the objects more complicated and it makes it hard to
build a valid return object without one.   Then functions need to all
be defined conditionally onw hether one's there or not if it's optional,
which is hard to debug and maintain and doc.

> * Should return value include timing information?
>
> Some people have asked for it, although currdently we don't do so programatically

This isn't a big deal.

> * There's no append_samples = <bool>
>
> OK
>
> * There's no option to compile the model from within the stan_nuts
>   call.
>
> I don't think there should be a stan_nuts() call, but either way, it should pass the compiled_model in.

OK.

> * data defaults to top-level environment with lazy read (not how
>   it's done now);  list is list of values as before
>
> I'll implement that for 2.7.0 since no one objected to what I posted before. It is technically the environments in R's lexical order rather than always the top-level environment.

Sorry -- I didn't mean top-level environment, I meant whatever
environment the RStan method/function was called from.

> * Instead of "chains" and a start ID, there's just a "chain_ids"
>
> Currently (and I think it should stay this way in the future) sampling() only does one chain, so it only needs to know the singular chain_id for the chain it is doing. Whatever is driving it whether it is in serial or parallel should be responsible for passing it the seed, chain_id, etc.

I'm guessing users like Andrew (or even me) are going to want something
that runs multiple chains and returns a single object on which we can print(),
plot(), and extract().  So I think this has to deal with multiple chains,
or at least we need top-level drivers that are included that do that.

> * Default num_warmup and num_samples very small by default (but shouldn't
>   be so small as to trigger scary messages about adaptation)
>
> Are you proposing changing the defaults of num_warmup and num_samples (1000 each)? If so, then we should do that for all the interfaces.

Yes, I think we agreed on 100 for all the interfaces.
We should make sure everyone agrees.  Too many people turn on 2000 and
then go away for the weekened.

> * Metric is specified by name of type or by value;  the names default
>   to unit values for init
> * Those adapt parameters are all for adapt_stepsize, right?
>
> Yeah, although I think the various configs should have their own class structure.

I agree.

> * Are there adaptation parameters for mass_matrix, like regularization?
>
> Not currently but we could add them.

I think we'd need to add them through the Stan C++ side
first.

Some of these questions were intended more generally, not about
the current state of RStan or 2.7.

> * params_to_save defaults to NA (or all), or a positive list of whole
>   parameter names.
>
> I'm not sure whether it is worth renaming the pars argument params_to_save, in part because in 2.7.0 there is an include = TRUE argument, so you could specify pars = "Sigma", include = FALSE to exclude Sigma but include everything else.

OK.

> * sample_file gets a copy of the output written to it, but return
>   object still created --- should this just move so that the return
>   object has a save on it?  Or should setting this cause the return of
>   this function to be NA?
>
> I think it should still return the regular stuff, in addition to writing the sample_file(s).
>
> mcmc_fit
> --------------------
>
>
> 3. EHMC
> ------------------------------------------------------------
> Plain old HMC looks just like NUTS, but with max_treedepth replaced
> by integration time:
>
> I would say they should be siblings in the class hierarchy for stan_config objects but get called the same way.

Looks like Michael strongly agrees with this.  We absolutely
have to get Michael's approval on whatever we call anything that
smacks of "HMC".  I'm very confused as to why Michael thinks
everyone's confused, but that's the nature of confusion.

> 4. Optimize
> ------------------------------------------------------------
>
> optimization_fit
> stan_lbfgs(
>
> Same deal. I think stan_lbfgs should be a class that inherits from stan_bfgs class with an additional slot for history_size but the user would call something like
>
> stan_optimize(compiled_program, config, data, init, verbose, ...)

OK --- I don't know what stan_bfgs is.  But in general, I don't like
the idea of lbfgs inheriting from bfgs because it's not an ISA relationship.
They could both inherit from a shared class that does what's in common, which
is how Michael has a lot of the MCMC classes set up in Stan C++.

> * Should verbose be a boolean?
>
> Yes
>
> * What does current as_vector do? Current doc says "flag indicating whether a
>   vector is used to for the point estimate found. A list can be
>   used instead by specifying it to be FALSE"
>
> If as_vector = TRUE, then only a vector of optimal parameters is returned. If as_vector = FALSE, then there is more stuff returned with the list.

Do we ever want as_vector = TRUE?  If not, let's get rid of it.
That is, if it's not too heavy, I think it's easier to return the whole
thing the same way all the time, then have an extractor or converter
for the result.

> * What's the behavior of tolerances if more than one's specified?  I'd
>   think it should be read as AND or as OR.
>
> Don't know.

This just needs to go in the doc.  It's explained in either the Stan
manual or the CmdStan doc, but I can never remember.

> * No option to specify parameter return as vector --- use a compiled

>
> But the compiled_model doesn't know what the optimal parameter values are. At least it doesn't currently.

Right, those would have to be passed in.

> optimization_fit
> --------------------
>     $par : parameters (as list)

>
> And $hessian optionally
>
> 5. Diagnose
> ------------------------------------------------------------
>
> diagnostics
> rstan::stan_diagnose(
>
> I think stan_diagnose should be a subclass of stan_config with epsilon and error_threshold that can be passed to stan_sample() or stan_optimize() like any other stan_config object.

Unless that subclass is a common subclass, then I don't like it
for the reasons above.  Only subclass for ISA relationships.

> diagnostics
> --------------------
> ?? not sure what should go in here --- it needs to be printable
>
> It doesn't exactly print (in the R sense currently) but the gradients get written to R's stream from C++. I don't think the gradients get saved anywhere currently, although we could do that.

If it returns an object, that object should have a print() method
and ideally a plot() method.  Then if you just call it without assigning,
it'll do the right thing and print, right?

- Bob

It seems like we agree on most things.

Discussion seems to be focused on:

- fragmentation/coagulation of configuration object and/or functions
- how thin should the stan_fit object be
- does "name" survive
- behavior of sample_file

We might keep in mind that we can probably accommodate some differences
between interfaces. For example, on `sample_file` I don't know of a
Python package that both returns values and writes out the same values
to a csv file in the same step (esp. in a world that's moving away from
CSV files and towards things like JSON and HDF5), but it probably
doesn't matter if one interface does something slightly different here.

(a few comments inline below)

Perhaps we can consolidate these on the Wiki? Including the points to be
resolved?

Best,

Allen

On 06/02, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> * Is there any reason to keep the name option?
> >
>
> I don't think it hurts anything and the name comes up in some of the
> printed output.
>
>

I'd vote emphatically for removing `name`. Models aren't generally named
in R or Python  -- we don't write lm0 <- lm(y ~ x, name="mymodel"). If
the user wants to name their model, they are free to do so. Insofar as
Stan is concerned, the identity of the model is the compiled model's C++
code (or the hash thereof).

> > * How long-lived is the "save_dso" option?
> >     - Where is it saved?
> >
>
> It is kind of confusing. The save_dso option currently just makes the dso

> to the disk to reuse it in a different session. But this is partially
> obsoleted by the 2.7.0 behavior if the auto_write option is enabled, in
> which case it is saving the compiled model object to the disk (in the same
> directory as the .stan file).
>

Is auto_write (aside: is this the best variable name?) going to be "on"
by default (yes!).

> ... <snip> ...

>
> > * sample_file gets a copy of the output written to it, but return
> >   object still created --- should this just move so that the return
> >   object has a save on it?  Or should setting this cause the return of
> >   this function to be NA?
> >
>
> I think it should still return the regular stuff, in addition to writing
> the sample_file(s).
>

Is there precedent for this in any R packages? I can't think of any
Python packages that do both.

Okay, a few meta comments:
The set_cppo() function (and doc) are currently gone because of the considerable probability of interfering with other R packages a user might install. I guess I should bring set_cppo() (and doc) back but only have it throw a warning that it doesn't do anything any more. We can put on the wiki instructions on how to modify ~/.R/Makevars but there is not much of a difference between -O3 and the default of -O2.
We can presumably create a class that combines the compiled code with R objects that correspond to the declarations in the data block of the .stan program. But currently I don't know exactly how to implement something like that in R code. My guess is that the code we have now does it, but in a transitory way since it is not a stand-alone thing.
I put a rough implementation of my "config S4 objects" idea in the other post https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-dev/jX-D619WW0o/K_okbvXaBKgJ . Those objects are not any bigger than they have to be in the sense that e.g. stan_bfgs only has BFGS-related slots but not num_warmup, etc. that are only relevant for MCMC.
If we internally need to pad a config object so that it has every possible configuration detail (even if the irrelevant ones are not accessed on the C++ side), then we could do that without involving the user.
About the ISA thing, it depends on what the definition of is is, and R defines it a bit differently than Java does. In this sense, a stan_lbfgs class "is" a stan_bfgs class because all of the slots of stan_bfgs are applicable to stan_lbfgs but stan_lbfgs adds one additional slot for history_size. So, the logic is more like "the child class includes everything that the parent class has, plus more" than a "the child class is a special case of the parent class". This does allow for minimally code validation because a stan_lbfgs has to be a valid stan_bfgs in addition to having a positive history_size. I think you are saying there should be a stan_bfgs_or_lbfgs class that is a parent of each, but then an object of stan_bfgs_or_lbfgs class can be created even though it is insufficient to know what to do with it (i.e. call the BFGS algorithm or the LBFGS algorithm).
Details ...

On Tuesday, June 2, 2015 at 2:01:41 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > * Is there any reason to keep the name option?
> >
> > I don't think it hurts anything and the name comes up in some of the printed output.
>
> What it hurts is readability of the doc and maintainability of
> the code.

I think those are minor relative to being to the print refering to "my_cool_model" rather than a md5 hash.

> > * Is it possible to save the DSO across sessions?
> >
> > Not for the cxxdso object per se but yes for the stanmodel object that has a slot for the cxxdso object.
>
> Would it be possible?  It would be super great if we had
> a DSO wrapper object and it was saveable, and an instantiated
> object that could be saved.

Maybe. I don't see much utility of saving the instantiated object with the data to the disk, since your data are presumably already saved to the disk along with the script that loads them. The good thing about the foo.rda files is that they are of negligible size on the disk.

> Then the idea's to do what Michael likes and have a big config object
> that works for everything --- optimization, MCMC, diagnosis, and whatever
> else comes up?  Or do you like breaking things out into sampling(),
> optimizing(), diagnosing(), vbing() etc.?
>
> I'd want to make things flatter, but I can live with this.

I think there should be sampling() and optimizing() --- perhaps with reverbing --- that would take each take a subset of stan_config classes. To my mind, VB is optimizing and just needs a (future) stan_vb config to distinguish it from ML. Both sampling() and optimizing() could accept a stan_diagnose config since at the moment it just streams the gradient comparison, but we could do something different if we ever had algorithm-specific diagnostics. Then stan_hmc, stan_rmhmc, etc. would be valid configs for sampling(). And if Michael needs us to utilize an uber-class internally to call the C++, then fine (this detail has never struck me as a big concern).

> With this, would we need the top-level stan() object to make
> people happy (again, I don't want to rip it out ASAP --- not until
> an RStan 3 was solidified).

Yeah, stan() would basically look the same but calling sampling() with config=new("stan_hmc") as many times as there are chains (optionally in parallel). I think it is no more fragile than Andrew's stan() function on mc-stan.org <http://mc-stan.org>.

> > * Default num_warmup and num_samples very small by default (but shouldn't
> >   be so small as to trigger scary messages about adaptation)
> >
> > Are you proposing changing the defaults of num_warmup and num_samples (1000 each)? If so, then we should do that for all the interfaces.
>
> Yes, I think we agreed on 100 for all the interfaces.
> We should make sure everyone agrees.  Too many people turn on 2000 and
> then go away for the weekened.

I agree that it should be the same for all interfaces. I would never call it with 100 because that is too few to do the convergence diagnostics I prefer. But more broadly, I disagree with the goal of making default arguments be optimal; default arguments should be on the safe side. If someone knows that they are doing MCMC in a situation where ML would work just fine, then they can tweak the options to reduce the runtime.

> > Plain old HMC looks just like NUTS, but with max_treedepth replaced
> > by integration time:
> >
> > I would say they should be siblings in the class hierarchy for stan_config objects but get called the same way.
>
> Looks like Michael strongly agrees with this.  We absolutely
> have to get Michael's approval on whatever we call anything that
> smacks of "HMC".  I'm very confused as to why Michael thinks
> everyone's confused, but that's the nature of confusion.

In my initial implementation, I made them be almost exactly like CmdStan, but if we are renaming CmdStan arguments to then we can rename them on the interface side.

> * What does current as_vector do? Current doc says "flag indicating whether a
>   vector is used to for the point estimate found. A list can be
>   used instead by specifying it to be FALSE"
>
> If as_vector = TRUE, then only a vector of optimal parameters is returned. If as_vector = FALSE, then there is more stuff returned with the list.

> Do we ever want as_vector = TRUE?  If not, let's get rid of it.
> That is, if it's not too heavy, I think it's easier to return the whole
> thing the same way all the time, then have an extractor or converter
> for the result.

If I were writing it from scratch, I wouldn't include an as_vector flag, but I'm not sure it is worth breaking any R code that might be using it.

> diagnostics
> --------------------
> ?? not sure what should go in here --- it needs to be printable
>
> It doesn't exactly print (in the R sense currently) but the gradients get written to R's stream from C++. I don't think the gradients get saved anywhere currently, although we could do that.

> If it returns an object, that object should have a print() method
> and ideally a plot() method.  Then if you just call it without assigning,
> it'll do the right thing and print, right?

Currently, I don't think C++ returns anything useful. It might be better to not stream but return the gradient comparison as a matrix that the user would have to print().

Ben

Couldn't one use the user-specific temporary files directory. I think
Windows, OS X, and Linux all have one. On Linux it's ~/.cache and on
Windows it is C:\users\username\AppData\Local\Temp

I'm strongly in favor of creating a LRU cache of compiled models in that
directory by default while making sure not to use more than N megabytes,
where N is the same as used by Chrome/Firefox by default for its
temporary files cache.

I think this would be a great feature and help us with some anecdotal
speed comparisons vis-a-vis other programs. I feel like people (myself
included) often are recompiling identical models because they forgot to
save them.

Best,

Allen

So it seems like there's another issue here we should discuss -- i.e.,
standard/recommended way to serializing and deserializing stan_model and
stan_fit objects.  Since if you need to get a full stan_fit object (or
stan_model object) there should definitely be a way to do that!

On the more narrow point about potentially getting rid of sample_file --
I think the proposed change would have the user in R or Python take
responsibility for writing the data in the stan_fit object to a csv file
after sampling/optimizing. We could provide a helper function to assist
the user -- but the rationale for the change would be that this writing
should be a separate step and not something done as part of the fitting.

Best,

Allen

through a function if it's not clear to the user what they're doing.

> 	• We can presumably create a class that combines the compiled code with R objects that correspond to the declarations in the data block of the .stan program. But currently I don't know exactly how to implement something like that in R code. My guess is that the code we have now does it, but in a transitory way since it is not a stand-alone thing.

I don't get the context for this.  I just want to be able
to grab:

 1.  compiled class for Stan program

 2.  class for Stan program instantiated with data

We must be doing at least (2) now because the functionality's there.
Or maybe it just gets reconsutructed each time?

> 	• I put a rough implementation of my "config S4 objects" idea in the other post https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-dev/jX-D619WW0o/K_okbvXaBKgJ . Those objects are not any bigger than they have to be in the sense that e.g. stan_bfgs only has BFGS-related slots but not num_warmup, etc. that are only relevant for MCMC.

Understood.

> 		• If we internally need to pad a config object so that it has every possible configuration detail (even if the irrelevant ones are not accessed on the C++ side), then we could do that without involving the user.

> 		• About the ISA thing, it depends on what the definition of is is,

The relevant definition of "is" is that "A is B" if and only if whatever
you can do with a B you can do with an A.  So it's not only having the same
slots, but having them mean the same thing.  That is, if you have A extend B,
then you should be able to run A as a B object to do everything B does and you
should be able to assign an A to a B reference.

> and R defines it a bit differently than Java does.

Java doesn't legislate this in its design and lots of people abuse
the inheritance hierarchy to do things that should be done with
encapulation.  That is, you see lots of people extend the library String
class to do things like add a number, so you get a String with a number.
That's not technically wrong if you think of your extension class as a String
with a number, but that's not usually what you want.

> In this sense, a stan_lbfgs class "is" a stan_bfgs class because all of the slots of stan_bfgs are applicable to stan_lbfgs but stan_lbfgs adds one additional slot for history_size. So, the logic is more like "the child class includes everything that the parent class has, plus more" than a "the child class is a special case of the parent class". This does allow for minimally code validation because a stan_lbfgs has to be a valid stan_bfgs in addition to having a positive history_size. I think you are saying there should be a stan_bfgs_or_lbfgs class that is a parent of each, but then an object of stan_bfgs_or_lbfgs class can be created even though it is insufficient to know what to do with it (i.e. call the BFGS algorithm or the LBFGS algorithm).

So there's no way to make a class purely abstract (and hence uninstantiatable)
as in Java or C++?

- Bob

> static-config-at-construction pattern we mostly use
> internally to Stan and I’m not sure how we’d design
> a parallel pattern for CmdStan.

The reason to make classes immutable is that it's easier to
guarantee they're always in safe and usable states.  And it
automatically makes them threadsafe, which would otherwise require
synchronization on the gets/sets.

It's often hard to do with getters/setters if you have linked
states to get and set.  For instance, if you have a class

  struct {
    real l_;
    real u_;
  }

with a constraint that l_ < u_, then you can't update that without
setting l_ and u_ at the same time because they're not independent
in validation.  The more interactions, the harder the getter/setter
design (and the harder the validation in general).

- Bob

Right, but a hierarchical config wouldn’t have any interactions
per say.  You could modify NUTS parameters even if NUTS
wasn’t the active HMC implementation.  In other words, you
have a big ol’ tree of parameters and the mutators would
ensure that each node has a valid value (validity being
defined by each parameter definition) and then at runtime
the config gets executed and selects out a single subtree
of active parameters.  Because the global tree is valid
each subtree will be valid.

Anyways, I’m just saying that a global config object
would be easy to manipulate safely.  It doesn’t get
around the overhead for learning a hierarchical
structure.  Also, there’s the interface consistency.
I think if we went with something like this we’d
have to not use methods but rather have functions
that take in a config class,

stan_config
stan_config.hmc.stepsize.set(0.0001)
sample(stan_config)

which would then roughly parallel the CmdStan
execution of

./model sample stan_config_string

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] proposal draft for RStan interface
messages.body_plain:
On Tuesday, June 2, 2015 at 7:41:26 PM UTC-4, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> I think if we went with something like this we’d
> have to not use methods but rather have functions
> that take in a config class,
>
> stan_config
> stan_config.hmc.stepsize.set(0.0001)
> sample(stan_config)
>
> which would then roughly parallel the CmdStan
> execution of
>
> ./model sample stan_config_string

I don't see the case for making the user deal with an object that has every possible configuration option. If the user wants to do HMC, then
config <- new("stan_hmc", stepsize = 0.0001) # is validated in R
print(config) # outputs something helpful but tailored to HMC
posterior <- sampling(model, config)
and then sampling() would internally coerce that config into whatever is needed by C++, including possibly filling in all the extra unused configuration options.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] proposal draft for RStan interface
messages.body_plain:
> > Are you proposing changing the defaults of num_warmup and num_samples (1000 each)? If so, then we should do that for all the interfaces.
>
> Yes, I think we agreed on 100 for all the interfaces.
> We should make sure everyone agrees.  Too many people turn on 2000 and

> then go away for the weekend.

I think 100 might be too small.  It might be fine for social science models
but for complex likelihoods (especially with ODEs) the adaptation typically
needs longer than 100.  I’d suggest 250 minimum, with a warning to users
that they might need more if they’re seeing poor sampling.

> Looks like Michael strongly agrees with this.  We absolutely
> have to get Michael's approval on whatever we call anything that
> smacks of "HMC".  I'm very confused as to why Michael thinks
> everyone's confused, but that's the nature of confusion.

Once again, the problem is that people currently equate “Hamiltonian
Monte Carlo” with what should more formally be called “Metropolis-corrected
Euclidean Hamiltonian Monte Carlo with static integration time”.  So when
you tweak any of those properties people think it’s a different algorithm
and we lose the concept of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo being this very
general approach.  This is a ubiquitous problem in MCMC  as it also
happens with Metropolis-Hastings (people confusing the general
Metropolis-Hastings construction vs particular proposals).

I want the naming to emphasize that any default is just _an_ implementation
of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo not _the_ implementation of Hamiltonian Monte
Carlo.  Having a “stan_hmc” option does the latter.

> We might keep in mind that we can probably accommodate some differences
> between interfaces. For example, on `sample_file` I don't know of a
> Python package that both returns values and writes out the same values
> to a csv file in the same step (esp. in a world that's moving away from
> CSV files and towards things like JSON and HDF5), but it probably
> doesn't matter if one interface does something slightly different here.

This is another thing that changes in the writer refactor as all
sample output gets passed to the interfaces piece by piece
by the callbacks.

But this does raise an important issue — in the new refactored
architecture each interface will be responsible for creating
writers and var_contexts which may or may not require their
own arguments.  So we can’t talk about a single config object
in isolation, rather we’ll have “internal” arguments and “interface”
arguments and we should keep this dichotomy in mind.

2.5).)

Best wishes,

Allen

aren't familiar with Markdown.

messages.subject: C++ namesapces: <cmath> is std:: <cmath>, <math.h> is ::
messages.body_plain:
There's a question down below.

I'm trying to remove all the uses of <math.h> in Stan because
it brings in functions in namespace ::, which pollutes all
other namespaces.

Alas, many functions (exp2, expm1, log1, log1p, etc.) are *not*
defined in <cmath> until C++11, but only exist in the C99-derived
<math.h>.  See:

  http://www.cplusplus.com/reference/cmath/

Everything works on the Mac clang++ side because they declare
those C++11 functions in <cmath> with the std:: namespace.  But
it doesn't work on Windows, which only defines them where the
spec says you'll find them, in <math.h>.

These functions are all defined by Boost in the Boost namespace.

I'm still trying to fight through getting max() to work in
size declarations and constraints for variables.

I'd like to remove <math.h>, but I'm worried about name conflicts
if I bring in the Boost versions with a using in the model (the way
we currently hack in lgamma).

QUESTION:  What should we do?

A1:  Follow lgamma and add a using statement for the Boost versions
to the generated Stan program code for each of these functions and
an include and using statement in the associated calls in rev and fwd
autodiff.

A2:  Define these problematic functions in stan::math as facades around
the Boost implementations so they get brought in with "using stan::math"
in the generated program code.

A3:  Define *all* of our functions in stan::math and fully qualify all
the calls in the generated code.  Rather than argument-dependent lookup,
all Stan function calls would be overloading of the same function in the
same namespace.  The user-defined functions would be qualified separately.

A4:  <your answer here>

With A1 or A2, when C++11 hits, we just get rid of the using statements (A1) or
definitions (A2).

I'm leaning toward A1 because it's less work.  It also forces us to
play nicely with everyone's namespaces.

What I worry about either way is that client code with "using namespace std" or
"include <math.h>" will make double-based versions of these calls ambiguous.

- Bob

My view is that ShinyStan is several orders of magnitude better than anything I could do statically in R, and what R can do statically is at least as good as what any other interface to Stan could do statically. So, we should concentrate on making it easy for someone, regardless of what Stan interface they used, to get their CSV output into ShinyStan via a web browser and not worry too much about plotting in the interfaces themselves.

If on the other hand, we did want to spend time beefing up the plotting capabilities of the interfaces, then it seems very difficult to standardize the plots. The only BSD plotting library that (I know of that) is any good is matplotlib, which now has a C++ interface

https://github.com/lava/matplotlib-cpp

I don't think it is worth doing, but it might be a good undergrad project.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Eigen preprocessor directives
messages.body_plain:
It's fine for a library (like Eigen) to mix LGPL and code that is more permissive licensed. But Stan is advertised as BSD, so we would have to more clearly distinguish what parts are BSD and what parts are LGPL if anything in Stan could ever be considered a derived work of LGPL code (patches to the LGPL parts of Eigen, inheriting from those classes, etc). I think it is the case that Stan is not currently using any of the LGPL Eigen code so the preprocessor directive would just prevent us from doing so in the future without recognizing it.

The other preprocessor directives are a bigger deal.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Eigen preprocessor directives
messages.body_plain:
Sounds good to me.  The Wikipedia seems pretty clear on
what's going on with LGPL --- it only copylefts itself :-)

  The GNU Lesser General Public License (LGPL) is a free software license
  published by the Free Software Foundation (FSF). The license allows developers
  and companies to use and integrate LGPL software into their own (even proprietary)
  software without being required by the terms of a strong copyleft license to release
  the source code of their own software-parts. The license requires that only the LGPL
  software-parts be modifiable by end-users via source code availability.

But if we can avoid it, we might as well not link to any of it if
we can avoid it.

End users of Stan can then change these properties and use the LGPL bits
and everything's fine, they just now have an LGPL + BSD (+Boost for boost,
+MPL2 for Eigen) product.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
There are two checks in integrate_ode that aren't necessary when using
CVODE:

 stan::math::check_ordered("integrate_ode", "times", ts);
 stan::math::check_less("integrate_ode", "initial time", t0, ts[0]);

Since CVODE can go backwards in time (but this tends to be a harder
problem to solve) and some of the problems I come across have
measurements associated with the initial condition.

How do you feel about removing those?

Kind regards,
Tom

messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] Computational Statistics in Python (re: PyMC3, PyStan)
messages.body_plain:
Here are some more thoughts on various topics.  Bottom line
is we should stay on our toes, but I think we'll be OK for
the foreseeable future.

This isn't so much just PyMC3, of course --- there are lots of
other packages out there with functionality very much overlapping
Stan's (BUGS, JAGS, Laplace's Demon, Church and its progeny,
Figaro, emcee, NONMEM, GPstuff, lme4, NIMBLE, INLA, etc. etc.).

METAPROGRAMMING

The key drawback for Stan is that we can't do any
metaprogramming relative to the Stan object language because
the Stan program itself isn't an object.

I'm genuinely curious what people would use it for.

I think this is an area that's really worth exploring.
It really struck me looking at Jeromy Anglin's workflow
for building and comparing multiple models in JAGS.  He
was reduced to cutting and pasting strings to swap in
and out priors, etc., which is pretty painful.

One thing we could do is define a graphical language within
Python and translate to Stan.  Perhaps even PyMC's if it's
decent --- I don't quite understand its boundaries from
the examples.  I was hoping we could piggyback on NIMBLE for
that in R.

FLEXIBILITY

Exactly what I'm trying to understand is how flexible
the PyMC modeling language is given that it's backed by
Theano.   Rob was digging around in the Python source today
trying to figure out which probability functions they
support.

I have the same question about Church, etc.

HARD WORK

Learning the Stan language involves work --- a lot of work to
learn it well.  I'd compare that to learning the PyMC structures
you need in Python.  In the end, assuming Python competence in
users and reasonable design choices, PyMC3 should be
less work to learn.

PyMC3 is also completely in-workflow --- you don't need to call
another language and have source files for it.  This is good, but
to the extent that we could define a model by a simple Python
structure, we might be able to swing something along these lines
ourselves.  In which case, it'd just come down to ease of installation
and who designed the better Python interface.

>From what I've seen, Stan's language is more direct for statistical
modeling, but is obviously way more limited in what it can do than
Python.  We can't stop and open up the Twitter API for more data in
the middle of a run, for instance --- I'm not sure if PyMC3 would
give you that kind of control (defining a variable in the model
as doing external work or getting updated asynchronously).

SPEED

Someone should measure this.  We've put a ton of effort into
our derivative speed and multivariates.  It'd be interesting
to see how PyMC3 compares.

FEATURES

Also consider things like constrained variables, covariance priors,
Cholesky factors, ODE solvers, etc.  These should all be possible
in something like PyMC3, but I have no idea to tell what they've
already implmented.

They certainly already have optimization, but I don't know if the
do the lm-like uncertainty estimation.  Of course, that'd be pretty
easy.

PORTABILITY

Stan models are portable across R, Python, command-line, etc.
That's good from a model-building community point of view, but
sub-optimal from an infrastructure perspective and it means we
have to do a ton of work as a team to field all these interfaces (the
point of the ongoing Stan 3 design and Allen's visit was to figure out
simpler interfaces without losing any power).

The same goes for platforms.  Windows is an ongoing pain, but there
are a lot of users there.  R's also been restricting what we can
do, as is Python to some extent in terms of moving to C++11, updating
dependent packages, structuring interface data types, etc.

For all we know, Julia's the future and Python and R are soon-to-be
zombies!  I'd rather hedge our bets on the platform choices.

 - Bob

messages.body_plain:
[I hijacked this thread from stan-users.]

There's a whole range of functionality surrounding diff eqs,
integrals, and optimization we'd like to add to Stan.

The first step for me is laying out what each of these would
look like in the language from a user's point of view.  Let's
talk about this at an upcoming Stan meeting --- I'd like to
understand where these things would be used.  They may also play
into a lot of what we're trying to do with VB, EP, MML, and related
optimization/approximation techniques.

The second step is understanding how to implement it.

Then the third step is getting it funded/finding time to do it.

What we need to do to get it funded is either (a) find a grant
dedicated to developing computational infrastructure (we have one and
just got another), or (b) find an application area that needs the
functionality and get the application and research into fitting the models
funded.  I'd like to roll a lot of this into an NIH grant that may target
both (a) and (b) together with PK/PD and other dynamic systems apps
in mind.

- Bob

...

I'm very much interested in a language for metaprogramming
models and it'd make sense to have that be native Python.

What I really want is modularity --- some way to take reasonable
programming practice to designing a model where you can test
a component as a module before plugging it into something larger.
Right now, our programs are big blobs.

But it'd be fun to brainstorm ideas in general as to what we
could do with metaprograms.

Does anyone know what people do with this capability in other
environments?

- Bob

can make it easy for users without installation.

Hello all,

I have finally got some time to get through writing up the first example of the BUGS book. Please find it attached. I think I have carried out all the steps which Bob wrote up on the github page. Before moving on to other examples, I wanted to get your feedback on the attached, as I am sure you will have preferences regarding content and style, as well as what I call the 'preferred' Stan model, which uses the most up-to-date thinking on priors, and coding style. I stopped short of building a beta-binomial model, as I allude to at the end, as I though this would be overkill, however, if you think this would be worthwhile, then I can look into it.

Once we have an agreed style in place, I don't think it will take as long to go through the various other examples, I hope.

Look forward to hearing your feedback - I'm sure there'll be plenty!

Best,

Ben

> > Firstly, divergences during warmup are ignorable as they usually typically
> > denote poor steps in the adaptation instead of pathologies in the sampler.
> > So if the divergences are really occurring only in the first 1000 iterations
> > then you’re fine.
> >
> > It’s only when you see divergences in the sampling phase that you have
> > to worry.  In this case manually specifying a step size will not be sufficient
> > because the adaptation will rapidly change the initial value (although
> > setting a lower step size can sometimes speed up adaptation if larger
> > step sizes lead to awkward parameter values and expensive likelihood
> > computations).  What you have to do is increase the target acceptance
> > probability (change “delta” parameter from the default 0.8 to 0.9 or
> > higher as necessary for removing the divergences).
> >

> > > > > Recall that we have two problems: is our fit parsimonious with the

> > > > > Fit the model to the simulated data

> > > > >  — if diagnostics fail improve model with a note explaining the fix

> > > > >  — if fit is poor then improve model with a note explaining the fix
> > > > >
> > > > > Step 2:

> > > > > Check posterior predictive checks
> > > > >  — if PPCs are bad improve model with a note explaining the fix

One of the main contributions of \OpenMx has been to encourage
treatment of statistical models and their components as things that
can be generated and manipulated within a programming environment.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] Computational Statistics in Python (re: PyMC3, PyStan)
messages.body_plain:
Theano deals well with matrices, at least for relatively basic stuff. (It knows things like ∂log|X|=X^{-1}, but I doubt that it knows obscure things like the differential of an eigenvalue or whatever.) It's the only package I know of that does. It is not, however, very focused on display, so it's better used for computation than derivation. (Theano is really optimized for neural networks, so dealing well with matrices isn't optional for them.)

Loops are a bit of a pain—they can handle them using their scan() function, but it's not very intuitive or well documented. But if you spent a day or so trying to understand how scan() works you could probably do things. Support for conditionals is limited, since everything needs to be done at compile time.

Matt

messages.body_plain:
Thanks --- that looks awesome.  Much more than we were
expecting.  Although it'd be great, the key thing is getting
the code for both the BUGS model and "best practices" model right.

Your updated model looks great!

As to the direct translation, it's fine as is, but it doesn't have
to be literally line for line.  I think it's OK to translate the model,
not the implementation.  So it's OK to use, for example, binomial_logit
in the translation.  This is really a judgment call, but I'd rather
err on the side of efficient Stan idioms as long as we literally
translate the model as written to one with the same posterior.
Maybe some bread crumbs in the text on the translation?

Then we want to provide the model we would've used.

Some specific comments:

* Num -> N

* keep the opening curly brace on the same line as the for statement
  (we basically follow the Google code style in Stan as well as in
   C++).

* spaces after commas (e.g., in gamma(0.001, 0.001))

* space between operators ("1 / sqrt(tau)" rather than "1.0/sqrt(tau)").

* Indentation in code needs to be right.  No tabs and everything
  indented 2 spaces.  You missed the indent on the binomial lines
  and all of the generated quantities block.  There's an emacs mode
  that'll clean this up for you automatically if you get everything
  on the right lines.  We're not entirely consistent yet in the manual
  and elsewhere, but we're aiming for it.

* I think instead of "1 / 1E-6" as your scale, you just want "1e3",
  that is, sd = 1 / sqrt(tau).

* I'd just define sigma <- 1 / sqrt(tau) as a transformed parameter
  and then use it in the student_t (sampling statement in model and
  rng in generated quantities), and eliminate sigma from generated quantities

* The fake data script is for the original model;  I'm not sure if
  we want it for both models or just our form?

* It'd be nice if we could do the simulation in Stan, too --- the R
  interface isn't really set up to do it very easily, but it's possible
  to run for a single iteration with generated quantities and no params and
  then pull out structured values --- just some awkward index fiddling.
  But then there's also something to be said for standalone fake data
  generation.

* always a space after commas, even in R

* Table 3 should be a plot with actual value on the x axis and fitted
  value with some interval on the y axis (geom_errorbars or something like
  that in ggplot2);  it could be faceted by top-level param name

* diagnostic discussion is great, but it should probably be 4.1, not 4.0.3.

* n_{\mathrm{eff}} and n_{\mathrm{leapfrog}} and \hat{R} in LaTeX

* I didn't understand the point of table 4 --- they're comparing different
  models and most of the BUGS entries are missing anyway

* The code after table 4 needs indentation

* Instead of

if (simTreatMort[i] > rt[i])
{

indicatorTreat[i] <- 1;
}
else
{

indicatorTreat[i] <- 0;
}

indent as

 if (simTreatMort[i] > rt[i]) {
   indicatorTreat[i] <- 1;
 } else {
   indicatorTreat[i] <- 0;
 }

but what you really want to do is this:

  indicatorTreat[i] <- (simTreatMort[i] > rt[i]);

* $p$-values, I think --- isn't the p usually italicized?  I don't
  know for sure as I don't do much with them.

* If you cite BDA, it should be BDA3

* Your bib form is messing up capitalization of journals for some reason

* Also, you need our fonts to get the code blocks right --- LaTeX messes
  up ~ as a matter of course in most fonts, conflating it with the diacritic
  tilde.

- Bob

>> Firstly, divergences during warmup are ignorable as they usually typically
>> denote poor steps in the adaptation instead of pathologies in the sampler.
>> So if the divergences are really occurring only in the first 1000 iterations
>> then you’re fine.
>>
>> It’s only when you see divergences in the sampling phase that you have
>> to worry.  In this case manually specifying a step size will not be sufficient
>> because the adaptation will rapidly change the initial value (although
>> setting a lower step size can sometimes speed up adaptation if larger
>> step sizes lead to awkward parameter values and expensive likelihood
>> computations).  What you have to do is increase the target acceptance
>> probability (change “delta” parameter from the default 0.8 to 0.9 or
>> higher as necessary for removing the divergences).
>>
