Two  of the checks appear ok: the value of Rhat < 1.1 for all parameters, and tree_depth<max_depth for all iterations. However, for the "n_divergent" parameter, I find that for about 10/2000 iterations this parameter is 1.
>>>
>>> Forgive me; this is probably due to my misunderstanding of the problem. I understand from reading the literature that this parameter indicates that the integrator is diverging during warm up (the first 1000 iterations). I have tried various re-parameterisations, as well as changing the priors (I have changed the scale parameter to be a cauchy(0,2.5) and tried using a normal rather than t prior for delta). I have also tried manually specifying a stepsize, to prevent the integrator stepping too far, but I cannot seem to prevent this divergence from occurring.
>>>
>>> Looking at the indices where the divergence occurs, it appears to happen frequently at iterations around: 2, 3, 4, 9, 102, 152, 252, 452, 952.
>>>
>>> I attach the RStan script file, which first generates simulated data, then fits the model to the simulated data. I also attach the Stan file, which has only been changed a bit vs the version on git. A finally attach the real data file.
>>>

>>> > On May 10, 2015, at 6:33 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:

>>> > I’d actually argue that simulations are paramount!

>>> > Recall that we have two problems: is our fit parsimonious with the
>>> > given model and is our model parsimonious with the “truth”?
>>> > Simulated data and our diagnostics checks the former, PPCs
>>> > check the latter.

>>> > I think it’d be great if for every example we had:

>>> > Step 1:
>>> > Simulate data from the model
>>> > Fit the model to the simulated data
>>> > Check diagnostics (n_divergent is zero for all iterations, tree_depth < max_depth for all iterations, R_hat < 1.1)

>>> > Check fit to exact results
>>> >  — if fit is poor then improve model with a note explaining the fix
>>> >

You don't really install an AMI; you just have to have an account to use it. But Amazon's gig is allowing people to rent exactly as much hardware as they need (which might include being able to do some stuff for free as long as you don't have to compile a model) but would mostly be for people whose laptops are not suitable for MCMC.

> Is SageMathCloud something that gives poeple free IPython Notebooks?
> If so, getting Stan on it would be awesome.  Allen --- could you
> help them get Stan implemented?

It (currently) gives people free accounts on the closest thing there is to a high-powered public server that happens to have IPython Notebooks. But an IPython Notebook is not specific to Python (which is why they are changing their name to Jupyter), so you could actually use any interface to Stan that was installed via an IPython Notebook. (IPython notebooks actually render on GitHub now, so it might be good to make one for each of the BUGS examples rather than a knitr document).

Ben

messages.subject: stan-dev@googlegroups.com vs stan-core@googlegroups.com
messages.body_plain:
We have two email lists (3 if you include stan-users). They have different permissions and serve slightly different purposes.

stan...@googlegroups.com:
- purpose: discussions about the development of Stan (this is really broadly defined)
- all emails are public and archived. The archive is also public.
- anyone is allowed to subscribe to the list
- anyone is able to browse through the history
- only people we allow are allowed to email the list. The have to be members of the list in order to post. (we're fairly liberal about who's allowed to post, but they have to care enough to ask us for permission)

stan...@googlegroups.com
- purpose: any discussion that is relevant to the people at the core of Stan, but mostly for private discussions or discussions with people that are not on the stan-dev list
- all emails are private and archived. The archive is available to current members.
- only people we allow are allowed to subscribe to the list
- only people we allow are able to browse the history
- anyone is allowed to email the list, even if they're not members

Andrew, if you want external people to participate on a discussion, it might be easier to send the discussion to stan...@googlegroups.com.

If anyone wants to change the permissions, we can discuss. I think it's worked out well for us so far, except for the few instances where we want external participants.

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Hi!

I finally got the Stan cvode branch up and running with the patch from Tom. Thanks again. I can confirm that the memory leak is gone. From the initial message of how long a single gradient evaluation takes it looks as if cvode takes 2-3 times as long as the boost solver. I have increased the tolerances to 1e-6 for relative and absolute error.

I am right now benchmarking the code on a large problem, let's see what happens, but it looks to me that we still need some tuning here. I will report once over - with boost my test case takes 3days per chain...

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Stiff ode solver
messages.body_plain:
> On Jun 22, 2015, at 5:34 AM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Yes, a test-suite would make a lot of sense. To report back: the cvode runs are far slower, but they seem to run more consistent, i.e. all chains progress at a very similar pace. The runs are not yet completed, I will report back once the runs are over.
>
> This puzzles me a bit, I hope cvode can be run in a faster way (I already went to 1e-6 absolute and relative tolerances).

I'd have only expected it to be faster if there was substantial
stiffness in the equations.  Otherwise, the Boost thing's doing far
less work per iteration.

> @Tom: Any suggestions? What parameters are important to take care of (Stan wise and cvode wise)?
>
> Out of curiosity: Is it thinkable to get
>
> http://headmyshoulder.github.io/odeint-v2/doc/boost_numeric_odeint/tutorial/parallel_computation_with_openmp_and_mpi.html
>
> up and running in Stan with the good old boost odeint integrator?

> The instructions sound very straightforward or am I overlooking something which prevents openMP for ODE solving in Stan fundamentally? Usually I get to hear "autodiff" is the killer, but isn't this now separate enough from autodiff?

This should be possible.  Our interface now just calls the ODE solver
with double values, so there's no race conditions with autodiff variables.
It may be possible to do the same with CVODE or other approaches, too.

I created a feature request and assigned it to Daniel, since this
is mostly going to be ODE and make-related (sorry, Daniel!):

  https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1511

We haven't been too worried about parallelism up until now because most
of our users fit modestly sized models on desktops/notebooks and have
at most four cores, which are fully occupied running four chains in
parallel.  But now that we're up against bigger models, putting each chain out
to a multiprocessor makes sense if we can manage.

- Bob

> >> Firstly, divergences during warmup are ignorable as they usually typically
> >> denote poor steps in the adaptation instead of pathologies in the sampler.
> >> So if the divergences are really occurring only in the first 1000 iterations
> >> then you’re fine.
> >>
> >> It’s only when you see divergences in the sampling phase that you have
> >> to worry.  In this case manually specifying a step size will not be sufficient
> >> because the adaptation will rapidly change the initial value (although
> >> setting a lower step size can sometimes speed up adaptation if larger
> >> step sizes lead to awkward parameter values and expensive likelihood
> >> computations).  What you have to do is increase the target acceptance
> >> probability (change “delta” parameter from the default 0.8 to 0.9 or
> >> higher as necessary for removing the divergences).

messages.body_plain:
Thanks --- that looks fantastic.  Are you generating the LaTeX
through knitr?

I like the plot with all the parameter values, but this style's going
to get problematic when the parameters aren't all on the same scale.
If I were doing it, I'd facet the different named parameters through
ggplot2.    But this is already way more than we need in this context,
so I'm not suggesting redoing it!

In general, I think 90% intervals are OK --- the problem is that
the larger the interval, the noisier the endpoint estimates are.

It's great that you plotted that we get the same result as BUGS.
Could you indicate if it's OpenBUGS or WinBUGS and which version?

The overlplotting of orange and blue (great color choice, by the
way) in the BUGS vs. Stan is a bit hard to read, but I don't think
it's a big deal.  What is an issue is that you probably want to be
comparing means +/- MCMC std error, as those are the things that should
converge to the same value if everything's working.

And to compare apples and apples, you need to do both with Stan's
method of computing n_eff.  I have some code to convert R2jags
output to something Stan can process.

The bibliography's still messed up in terms of capitalization.
(And "2x 2" rather than "2 x 2".)

You want to use "a---b" for em-dashes to separate text in
American English typesetting (you get an extra space in the UK,
but you also want to use the em-dash).

The values 1 and 0 shouldn't be quoted.  A quote usually
indicates a character rather than the value.

Spaces, so it's not [0.025,0.975], but [0.025, 0.975].

And remember, 95% intervals are going to be noisier than,
say 80% intervals.  In both cases, you can calibrate by eye.

Sorry for all the typesetting comments --- I'm a nut about it,
but it's all minor stuff compared to the content.

- Bob

P.S.  Some R to fit a JAGS model (for an IRT example) and then
pull out the effective sample sizes.  It's not complete, as
there are dependencies on things like num_params, but I hope it's
clear what's going on (the relevant bit is the monitor and n_eff
extraction, which Ben showed me how to do):

start_time_jags <- proc.time();

fit_jags <- jags(model.file = "irt.jags",
                 data = list(I=I, J=J, y=y),
                 init = init_list,
                 parameters.to.save = c("alpha","beta","delta"),
                 n.chains = num_chains,
                 n.iter = 10000,
                 jags.seed = init_seed);

elapsed_time_jags = proc.time() - start_time_jags;
print(c("jags", elapsed_time_jags));

fit_jags_mcmc <- as.mcmc(fit_jags);
arr <- as.array(fit_jags_mcmc);
arr <- aperm(arr, c(1,3,2));
mon <- monitor(arr, inc_warmup = FALSE);

n_eff_jags <- mon[1:num_params, "n_eff"];
sec_jags <- elapsed_time_jags[3];
n_eff_per_sec_jags <- n_eff_jags / sec_jags;

> In general, I think 90% intervals are OK --- the problem is that
> the larger the interval, the noisier the endpoint estimates are.

Yep, I will redo these with those intervals.

> It's great that you plotted that we get the same result as BUGS.
> Could you indicate if it's OpenBUGS or WinBUGS and which version?

Yes, I will include this information, FYI it's OpenBUGS. version 3.2.3. rev 1012.

>

> way) in the BUGS vs. Stan is a bit hard to read, but I don't think

>
> it's a big deal.  What is an issue is that you probably want to be

Ok. I will redo with the plot with these.

> output to something Stan can process.

I'm not sure I follow you. Your code makes sense for extracting n_eff from JAGS output, but how will I use this as an input for Stan? Sorry, I think this is somewhat due to my poor knowledge of n_eff; I know that it is an effective sample size essentially measures the number of independent iterations from mcmc, but unsure how to specify this a priori for Stan.

>
> The bibliography's still messed up in terms of capitalization.
> (And "2x 2" rather than "2 x 2".

Ok, is there a style that you recommend? At the moment I am just using 'plain'.

> You want to use "a---b" for em-dashes to separate text in
> American English typesetting (you get an extra space in the UK,
> but you also want to use the em-dash).
>
> The values 1 and 0 shouldn't be quoted.  A quote usually
> indicates a character rather than the value.

Ok.

>
> Spaces, so it's not [0.025,0.975], but [0.025, 0.975].
>

Yep, my mistake. Will change.

> And remember, 95% intervals are going to be noisier than,
> say 80% intervals.  In both cases, you can calibrate by eye.
>
> Sorry for all the typesetting comments --- I'm a nut about it,
> but it's all minor stuff compared to the content.
>
> - Bob
>
> P.S.  Some R to fit a JAGS model (for an IRT example) and then
> pull out the effective sample sizes.  It's not complete, as
> there are dependencies on things like num_params, but I hope it's
> clear what's going on (the relevant bit is the monitor and n_eff
> extraction, which Ben showed me how to do):
>
> start_time_jags <- proc.time();
>
> fit_jags <- jags(model.file = "irt.jags",
>                  data = list(I=I, J=J, y=y),
>                  init = init_list,
>                  parameters.to.save = c("alpha","beta","delta"),
>                  n.chains = num_chains,
>                  n.iter = 10000,
>                  jags.seed = init_seed);
>
> elapsed_time_jags = proc.time() - start_time_jags;

>
> fit_jags_mcmc <- as.mcmc(fit_jags);
> arr <- as.array(fit_jags_mcmc);

messages.body_plain:
I don't think Stan's ready for C++11 to be turned on
by default or even not by default because it'll break
CRAN compatibility.  (Ben should know more).  And it'll
break everything forced to use older compilers, including
R and any other project that forces older compiler versions.

But there's no reason we can't play around with it in experimental
branches.  Or provide some way to modify.

The problem is that we don't want to just keep pasting on
dependencies and ifdefs, and whatnot --- the dependencies are
already killing us.

- Bob

Thanks.  I should try to intsall OpenBUGS and see how it compares
to JAGS in terms of speed.  So far, all we know is this:

  https://martynplummer.wordpress.com/2010/09/20/how-fast-is-jags/

Martyn rescales by dividing time by the mean effective sample size.
We're not sure what the right way to compare is.

> The overlplotting of orange and blue (great color choice, by the
> way) in the BUGS vs. Stan is a bit hard to read, but I don't think
> it's a big deal.  What is an issue is that you probably want to be
> comparing means +/- MCMC std error, as those are the things that should
> converge to the same value if everything's working.
>
> Ok. I will redo with the plot with these.
>
> And to compare apples and apples, you need to do both with Stan's
> method of computing n_eff.  I have some code to convert R2jags
> output to something Stan can process.
>
> I'm not sure I follow you. Your code makes sense for extracting n_eff from JAGS output, but how will I use this as an input for Stan?

Some of those commands are for rstan --- that was a complete
example of pulling n_eff out for JAGS output --- presumably the
same thing would work for BUGS if they have Coda-compatible output.

> Sorry, I think this is somewhat due to my poor knowledge of n_eff; I know that it is an effective sample size essentially measures the number of independent iterations from mcmc, but unsure how to specify this a priori for Stan.

The point is that we do n_eff estimates more conservatively in
Stan than in packages like Coda, which the R packages for BUGS
and JAGS use.  That leads to bigger MCMC std error estimates,
because they're just

  mcmc_std_err = posterior_sd / sqrt(n_eff)

But this isn't critical here, so you could just use the BUGS
versions of mcmc std err (if they have them).

Overall, I'm still not sure we should be comparing to BUGS as
part of these writeups.  One, we don't want to give the impression
that BUGS is somehow the "reference" answer --- we trust Stan more
to do the right thing in the tails and for hard models.

On the other hand, part of the motivation is to reassure people
who trust BUGS that Stan can be trusted, too.

> The bibliography's still messed up in terms of capitalization.
> (And "2x 2" rather than "2 x 2".
>
> Ok, is there a style that you recommend? At the moment I am just using 'plain'.

I don't care as long as it capitalizes properly!  For
the manual, we use:

\bibliographystyle{apalike}
\makeatletter
\renewcommand\@biblabel[1]{}
\makeatother
\bibliography{../bibtex/all}

I don't have the exact example coded up in ggplot2.  What you want
to do is something like facet_wrap(~ parameter) in a data frame with
all the params.  Here's an example I did of plotting Stan vs. JAGs
times for all paramters (as opposed to just averaging):

df_stan <- data.frame(n_eff_per_sec = n_eff_per_sec_stan,
                      parameter = param_names,
                      mcmc = rep("stan", num_params));

df_jags <- data.frame(n_eff_per_sec = n_eff_per_sec_jags,
                      parameter = param_names,
                      mcmc = rep("jags", num_params));

df <- rbind(df_stan, df_jags);

library(ggplot2);
plot <- ggplot(df, aes(x = n_eff_per_sec, fill = mcmc)) +
        geom_histogram() +
        scale_x_log10() +
        facet_wrap(~ parameter) +
        ggtitle("Stan vs. JAGS: IRT 2PL, 20 questions (I), 200 students (J)") +
        xlab("n_eff / sec") +
        ylab("# parameters");

messages.body_plain:
Hi!

First of all I want to say that this is really great! We need this type really bad and what you produced is really good stuff I think. Some comments:

1. I think it would be good to make the BUGS engine exchangeable, i.e. the user should be able to switch between WinBUGS (the mother of all BUGS), OpenBUGS and JAGS. There should be R packages out there which are of help here.

2. Before you move on to other examples I suggest to think about how all of the example can later on be processed in an automatic fashion, i.e. I am thinking of something similar (but more sophisticated) like the stan_demo function. Basically I would appreciate if one can get all these nice example models in a programmatic way as other people prefer different comparisons.

3. The way I once came up with to compare Stan vs WinBUGS output was the following:
- I declared WinBUGS as reference which is what you want to do as this type of work in anyway only for WinBUGS followers
- Then I standardize each quantity of interest from the models with respect to the median and robust standard deviation (inter-quantile-range divided by 1.34) such that the WinBUGS output and the Stan output becomes roughly standard normal
- Last, I computed the 2.5%, 5% ... 95%, 97.5% quantiles from each program and then checked that the absolute difference is below 0.1

4. The simulation of the fake data should be done somehow with the fixed_param algo from rstan as Bob points out.

Could we place this stuff in some git repo? This makes it easier to track the code & interact. My third point is something which really does not need to be part of this, but I would really appreciate if I could do this type of stuff with this work given that point 2 is taken care of.

Really cool!

Best,
Sebastian

I’m not sure what that means either. I can add a test to see if variational inference prints anything to standard output (which may be what Kui means?).

The name of the CmdStan top-level equivalent is currently `experimental variational`, e.g., `./bernoulli experimental variational data file=bernoulli.data.R`. It is under `experimental` at the moment because I believe EP was supposed to be (or is) as well.

I tend to agree on the comments about the ADVI name. It’s nice that it emphasizes one of the primary features that distinguishes our variational inference from other implementations. However, there are other primary features in place too, e.g., parameter transformations, and there will be many other excellent features in the future such as my long term goal of putting in copulas to generally learn the dependency structure among the latent variables. I personally like “automatic variational inference”, as in the title of the preprint and which follows the motivation of probabilistic programming more closely. Regardless, Alp has been spearheading the project from the get-go, and I’m happy to stick by whatever he decides to name it.

Dustin

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for reposting on stan-dev.

The first order of business is to create an issue.  Ideally
this will come with a test that fails.  Feel free to actually
write it as a test in a branch and then we can work on the fix
in that branch.

We do not want any fixes that do not come with unit tests
that (a) fail in the old version, and (b) pass in the new.

I don't even know if this is a CmdStan or Stan issue right
now given the fluid nature of the command code recently.

Nothing should be testing cin or cout, but should instead
use passed-in stringstreams to collect answers.

Daniel will hopefully know how to fix the problem.

And by the way, this is why we like those completely broken
tests that just make sure output's getting through.  (They're
broken because they're typically hardwired to exact output rather
than more functional.)

- Bob

> Hi!

> First of all I want to say that this is really great! We need this type really bad and what you produced is really good stuff I think. Some comments:
>
> 1. I think it would be good to make the BUGS engine exchangeable, i.e. the user should be able to switch between WinBUGS (the mother of all BUGS), OpenBUGS and JAGS. There should be R packages out there which are of help here.

The languages are not the same, so it would mean
rewriting the models.

> 2. Before you move on to other examples I suggest to think about how all of the example can later on be processed in an automatic fashion, i.e. I am thinking of something similar (but more sophisticated) like the stan_demo function. Basically I would appreciate if one can get all these nice example models in a programmatic way as other people prefer different comparisons.

It wasn't clear to me what you're asking for here.  Could you provide
an example?

> 3. The way I once came up with to compare Stan vs WinBUGS output was the following:
> - I declared WinBUGS as reference which is what you want to do as this type of work in anyway only for WinBUGS followers

I'd prefer not to describe WinBUGS as a reference in anything we
write.

> - Then I standardize each quantity of interest from the models with respect to the median and robust standard deviation (inter-quantile-range divided by 1.34) such that the WinBUGS output and the Stan output becomes roughly standard normal

You mean posterior median of a parameter?   And what's the inter-quantile
range that you're dividing by 1.34?

I don't think this makes sense from an MCMC perspective, which
gives you guarantees on the means and error from the MCMC CLT.

> - Last, I computed the 2.5%, 5% ... 95%, 97.5% quantiles from each program and then checked that the absolute difference is below 0.1

My own preference is to make the comparison with WinBUGS output
a completely separate project.

You need to run a lot of iterations to get good 2.5% intervals.
And this is likely to be where we disagree with BUGS by getting
more into tails.  And this is also why Gibbs shouldn't be the gold
standard.  See the Betancourt and Girolami paper on hierarchical
models.

I would also strongly prefer to do synthetic code generation for
tests so that we know the answer rather than relying on comparisons
with BUGS.

But all this can be in a separate project.  What we really need
are the models translated as a first priority.

> 4. The simulation of the fake data should be done somehow with the fixed_param algo from rstan as Bob points out.
>
> Could we place this stuff in some git repo?

Agreed.  Ben --- we can give you push permission if you give us your
GitHub handle.  For us, nothing exists that's not in GitHub.

messages.subject: weighted log-likelihood
messages.body_plain:
Andrew (mostly): Do we want stan_glm() to throw an error if weights are passed? In general, we want stan_glm() to accept all the same arguments as glm(), but we could make an exception if something would be objectively wrong from a Bayesian perspective. The glm() function allows weights to be any non-negative vector and clarifies that

> Non-NULL weights can be used to indicate that different observations have different dispersions (with the values in weights being inversely proportional to the dispersions); or equivalently, when the elements of weights are positive integers w_i, that each response y_i is the mean of w_i unit-weight observations. For a binomial GLM prior weights are used to give the number of trials when the response is the proportion of successes: they would rarely be used for a Poisson GLM.

So, which if any, of those possibilities should stan_glm() allow? It seems that negative or non-integer weights should definitely not be allowed.

Similarly, for stan_lm vs. lm, the weights are described as
> If non-NULL, weighted least squares is used with weights weights (that is, minimizing sum(w*e^2)); otherwise ordinary least squares is used. Non-NULL weights can be used to indicate that different observations have different variances (with the values in weights being inversely proportional to the variances); or equivalently, when the elements of weights are positive integers w_i, that each response y_i is the mean of w_i unit-weight observations (including the case that there are w_i observations equal to y_i and the data have been summarized).

Ben

We're much more laid back on the stan-dev/example-models repo,
which is where this should go.

The best way to get things reviewed going forward is through pull
requests.  Then it's easy to leave notes in the code.

There are already BUGS models there and we want to remove
the old ones and insert the new ones.

My main goal for this is to

a) show people how to directly translate the BUGS models,

b) make sure they know we don't condone the BUGS priors,
   and

c) provide an example of how we think the models should be
   written.

Of these, (c) is most important for us (that is the Stan dev
team).  But I understand lots of people are interested in (a)
for both speed comparisons (why you want to make the BUGS models
good implementations) and to satisfy themselves we're getting
the same answers.

After that, I think it'd be great if we could figure out a
way to unit test all these.  But that's something we need to
figure out in general, not for this immediate project.

- Bob

P.S.  I sent you an invite to give you permission to push to
example-models.

messages.subject: what do do about weights in tan_regression
messages.subject_clean: what do do about weights in tan_regression
messages.body_plain:
Yah, good point.  Perhaps best to just disallow weights for now.  Zero weights are easy enough, of course, but it seems like more trouble than we need to allow them.

Alternatively we could allow weights, as Bob suggests, but then spit out lots of warnings.  The trouble with disallowing weights is that a lot of users will want them.  Also, if weights are fairly mild, it shouldn’t be so horrible to include them.

As I told Bob, suppose someone supplies a dataset with weights of 1000, 1000, 1000, 1000, etc.  Compared to weights of 1, 1, 1, 1, etc., the result won’t affect the MLE, but they will change any informative-prior Bayes estimate (by giving 1000x the weight to the likelihood) and also it will result in tiny standard errors (and, depending on the model, possible poor convergence of HMC).  Bob suggested rescaling the weights to sum to N, but that won’t in general work, as can be seen from the example of a simple logistic regression where three items each have weights of 1 and the other N-3 items have weight of 1e-6 each.  The result will be to give each of the three items a weight of N/3 each, implying much stronger data than actually exist.  (Things are a bit trickier with linear regression because of the free-floating variance parameter.)

The long story is that, from a Bayesian perspective, there’s really no such thing as weighted regression.  So we’re in a bit of a bind in how we compromise this.

We have another such compromise issue when we want to do point estimation.  For logistic regression, ordered logit, probit, Poisson, neg binomial, etc etc etc., standard practice is MLE and we can do that too, or even better we can do posterior mode.  But for linear regression, standard practice is to use the 1/(N-K) denominator on the variance, and I’ve struggled to see how to come up with this answer generically (without “cheating” and having the program know that it’s linear regression).  Not an issue with full Bayes but it comes up if we want to have point estimation for compatibility.

For now I guess we should follow Bob’s advice and use increment_log_prob() with weights, and when weights are specified in stan_regression, we spit out a warning and also print out the sum of the weights.

On Tuesday, June 23, 2015 at 11:07:01 PM UTC-4, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> For now I guess we should follow Bob’s advice and use increment_log_prob() with weights, and when weights are specified in stan_regression, we spit out a warning and also print out the sum of the weights.

I guess there are several situations:
For MLE that happens to use Stan's optimization algorithm, I think it is self-evident that stan_foo() should handle the weights in the same way as foo().
For penalized MLE, MCMC, and things like that, we could follow Bob's suggestion (presumably  disallowing negative weights), but I have a hard time coming up with any rationale for non-integer weights in a Bayesian GLM.
For the case where glm() does "For a binomial GLM prior weights are used to give the number of trials when the response is the proportion of successes", that also makes complete sense from a Bayesian perspective (provided weight[i] * y[i] is an integer). Sometimes medical data comes this way because they don't want to individually identify the successes and failures.
More generally, in any case where the weights are non-negative integers and represent the number of cases observed in the sample with that data, I wouldn't mind throwing an error that says, in effect, "duplicate each row i weight[i] times and try again without weights".
Generalized Least Squares is Ordinary Least Squares on transformed data, so it doesn't seem particularly problematic from a Bayesian perspective to do a Gaussian model on the transformed data.

Other opinions?

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Regarding the diagnostics:

The n_leapfrog isn’t technically what you want to be looking for, and is
mostly redundant with treedepth anyways, so I’d just look at divergences
and treedepth.  I actually like showing a histogram of treedepth here, with
a line at 10, but this count is fine.

Also you have to be really careful with the language — the diagnostics
passing do not indicate convergence/mixing but rather show no signs of
non-convergence/non-mixing.  This is a subtle but important point as
we can never guarantee convergence.

Additionally you don’t quote how many chains you run.  I’d make this
explicit in the call and emphasize the robustness given by running
multiple chains.

> The overlplotting of orange and blue (great color choice, by the
> way) in the BUGS vs. Stan is a bit hard to read, but I don't think
> it's a big deal.  What is an issue is that you probably want to be
> comparing means +/- MCMC std error, as those are the things that should
> converge to the same value if everything's working.

As Bob noted we really want to be treating Stan as the baseline and
(hoping) that we’re geometrically ergodic so the MCMC std error means
something.  Assuming that this is true then what I’d recommend is

(a) rescale each parameter by subtracting the Stan mean and then
dividing by the Stan MCMC std error.

(b) The Stan parameters are all now N(0, 1) and can be represented
by a solid band from -2 to 2.

(c) Now you can plot the BUGS results as points + bars representing
the standardized means +/- 2 standardized deviations.  Everything will
be on a consistent scale and deviations will be easy to spot.

You can do a similar resealing with the simulated data, only given that
the simulated data is exact you won’t need a band (just a line at 0) and
you’d want to use posterior quantiles (as you already do in Figure 1).
It would be great to see this particular plot for both Stan and BUGS.

Additionally Bob noted that performance is important.  I recommend
adding a quick “Performance” section and plotting histograms of
n_eff / time for all parameters, one histogram for BUGS and one for
Stan.  This can be done by overlapping transparent histograms on
one plot or just having two separate figures.

Hi Bob!

To your points:

1. If you write the BUGS models with a bit of care, then they can be run with any of the three BUGS flavors. Just checkout the BUGSExamples package from Martyn Plummer. Only a handful of models need a single line of code different to run on JAGS.

2. I would like to be able to do something like this:

bugs_demo("winbugs_example_xy", engine="Stan") # this runs the "best practices" example in Stan; of course, the Stan engine will be the default
bugs_demo("winbugs_example_xy", engine="JAGS") # this runs the "best practices" example in JAGS or OpenBUGS or WinBUGS
bugs_demo("winbugs_example_xy", engine="JAGS", data="fake") # this runs the "best practices" example in JAGS or OpenBUGS or WinBUGS on fake data (which is also returned)
bugs_demo("winbugs_example_xy_vanilla", engine="JAGS") # this runs the vanilla example in JAGS or OpenBUGS or WinBUGS

3. This is really something which I do not ask for inclusion in this exercise here, but rather would like to be able to program it myself given that step 2 is done. Maybe a better wording is "with respect to the WinBUGS" result? The basic idea I am proposing is to first standardize the samples using robust estimators of the location and dispersion. This is essentially the same what Michael is suggesting and it effectively makes the 2-sample problem a 1-sample problem which is ok in this case, I think. And yes, going down to 2.5% and up to 97.5% requires a large sample size - using normal approximations one can get a handle on this.

Of course, the 2.5% steps are an arbitrary choice (one could even randomize this z-range which is compared), but then, the 95% is the magic number which is old, yes, but certainly used very often such that it is still up to date - at least for the people who are looking into this.

Best,
Sebastian

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] py_var_context
messages.body_plain:
> Cython can definitely do what RStan does --- create something that
> exposes a dict-interface with lazy fetching.
>
> I might not be understanding the concern correctly -- but isn't delaying
> reading the data here a potentially bad thing? Isn't having an immutable
> version of the data a good thing?

Firstly I don’t think immutable var_contexts are going to be flexible
enough for every use case.  I’m thinking in particular on the C++ side
where it’d be much easier to create a var context and then add data
one-by-one, a la

var_context context;
context.add_parameter(“name1”, values1, dims1);
context.add_parameter(“name2”, values2, dims2);
context.add_parameter(“name3”, values3, dims3);

Secondly, lazy querying is handy because users can add unnecessary
data into the source file/environment without incurring any I/O overhead.
For example, say someone wanted to put data, inits, and a metric all in
the same file.  Lazy querying would allow us to create three different
var contexts using the same source but only load each parameter once
instead of in triplicate.  Also this would open up the possibility of using
the local environment as a source instead of having to pass everything
in by hand.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] py_var_context
messages.body_plain:
I don't think var_context itself should even have an implementation.
So some of the implementations can be just thin shells around
environments or dictionaries and we can also have a setter/getter
container like Michael's suggesting below.

In addition to what Michael said, the laziness only lasts until
data read time.  At that point it gets read into the Stan model
object at construction time.  This is the same point at which RStan
or CmdStan do validation, so there's no clean way to guarantee
behavior.

I just pasted the second response inline below.

> On Jun 24, 2015, at 7:18 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Allen,
>

> The big difference is in the internals.  RStan uses an RList object internally which can be lazily queried for variables.

That's in the future, right?  Because now it'll balk if there's
other junk in the environment with NA values.

>  CmdStan (dump.hpp) read in a text file, parses the parameters, and then stores everything in internal memory upon construction.  PyStan parses all of the parameters into vectors externally and then passes them into the var context on construction.
>
> Does Cython have an RList equivalent?  Something that would wrap a dict and allow it to be queried lazily?

Do we also want to wrap environments in Python?  I'm happy
not doing that as it pollutes environments if they're global
as most people use these things.

Julia appears to have the same issues with C++ as Python, but
so far, Stan.jl is a wrapper around CmdStan rather than integrating
at the C++ level.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I worry tremendously about feature creep leading to relatively
simple and useful projects never getting finished because they
won't hit the ultimate goal.

Project 1
-------------
It would be very useful to us to just have the Stan versions
of the BUGS models rewritten --- direct translation and
the model we think is better.  And by direct translation, I mean
no-holds-barred best way we can code it in Stan to get
the same posterior.  And I mean just the models.  Nothing else.
No LaTeX, no comparisons with BUGs, etc. etc.

Project 1.5
---------------
Writing up nice doc for all these models explaining why the Stan
models are the way they are to help BUGS users program in Stan.
Note that this does not need comparison with BUGS output.

Project 2
--------------
Generating an R package that runs models in Stan, WinBUGS,
OpenBUGS, JAGS, Laplace's demon, MCMCpack, and anything else people
want to throw at it.  Hopefully the dependencies can be optional for that.

Project 3
-------------
Comparison with BUGS (JAGS, OpenBUGs, ...?).  There are really
two related things here.

We (the Stan devs, that is), would much prefer to do this on our
own turf writing models the way we want them for all the reasons
Michael has laid out computationally and Andrew has laid out
statistically.

Sebastian I believe wants to compare the BUGS models as written
by BUGS (or perhaps as translated by Martyn Plummer to JAGS --- I
was surprised about the flexiblity here --- I'd think the original
WinBUGS models would be a requirement).

- Bob

> On Jun 24, 2015, at 7:04 AM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Bob!
>
> To your points:
>
> 1. If you write the BUGS models with a bit of care, then they can be run with any of the three BUGS flavors. Just checkout the BUGSExamples package from Martyn Plummer. Only a handful of models need a single line of code different to run on JAGS.
>
> 2. I would like to be able to do something like this:
>
> bugs_demo("winbugs_example_xy", engine="Stan") # this runs the "best practices" example in Stan; of course, the Stan engine will be the default
> bugs_demo("winbugs_example_xy", engine="JAGS") # this runs the "best practices" example in JAGS or OpenBUGS or WinBUGS
> bugs_demo("winbugs_example_xy", engine="JAGS", data="fake") # this runs the "best practices" example in JAGS or OpenBUGS or WinBUGS on fake data (which is also returned)
> bugs_demo("winbugs_example_xy_vanilla", engine="JAGS") # this runs the vanilla example in JAGS or OpenBUGS or WinBUGS
>
> 3. This is really something which I do not ask for inclusion in this exercise here, but rather would like to be able to program it myself given that step 2 is done. Maybe a better wording is "with respect to the WinBUGS" result? The basic idea I am proposing is to first standardize the samples using robust estimators of the location and dispersion. This is essentially the same what Michael is suggesting and it effectively makes the 2-sample problem a 1-sample problem which is ok in this case, I think. And yes, going down to 2.5% and up to 97.5% requires a large sample size - using normal approximations one can get a handle on this.
>
> Of course, the 2.5% steps are an arbitrary choice (one could even randomize this z-range which is compared), but then, the 95% is the magic number which is old, yes, but certainly used very often such that it is still up to date - at least for the people who are looking into this.
>
> Best,
> Sebastian
>
> On Wednesday, June 24, 2015 at 12:42:36 AM UTC+2, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>>> On Jun 23, 2015, at 3:33 PM,
>>>
>>> Hi!
>>>
>>> First of all I want to say that this is really great! We need this type really bad and what you produced is really good stuff I think. Some comments:
>>>
>>> 1. I think it would be good to make the BUGS engine exchangeable, i.e. the user should be able to switch between WinBUGS (the mother of all BUGS), OpenBUGS and JAGS. There should be R packages out there which are of help here.
>>
>> The languages are not the same, so it would mean
>> rewriting the models.
>>
>>> 2. Before you move on to other examples I suggest to think about how all of the example can later on be processed in an automatic fashion, i.e. I am thinking of something similar (but more sophisticated) like the stan_demo function. Basically I would appreciate if one can get all these nice example models in a programmatic way as other people prefer different comparisons.
>>
>> It wasn't clear to me what you're asking for here.  Could you provide
>> an example?
>>
>>> 3. The way I once came up with to compare Stan vs WinBUGS output was the following:
>>> - I declared WinBUGS as reference which is what you want to do as this type of work in anyway only for WinBUGS followers
>>
>> I'd prefer not to describe WinBUGS as a reference in anything we
>> write.
>>
>>> - Then I standardize each quantity of interest from the models with respect to the median and robust standard deviation (inter-quantile-range divided by 1.34) such that the WinBUGS output and the Stan output becomes roughly standard normal
>>
>> You mean posterior median of a parameter?   And what's the inter-quantile
>> range that you're dividing by 1.34?
>>
>> I don't think this makes sense from an MCMC perspective, which
>> gives you guarantees on the means and error from the MCMC CLT.
>>
>>> - Last, I computed the 2.5%, 5% ... 95%, 97.5% quantiles from each program and then checked that the absolute difference is below 0.1
>>
>> My own preference is to make the comparison with WinBUGS output
>> a completely separate project.
>>
>> You need to run a lot of iterations to get good 2.5% intervals.
>> And this is likely to be where we disagree with BUGS by getting
>> more into tails.  And this is also why Gibbs shouldn't be the gold
>> standard.  See the Betancourt and Girolami paper on hierarchical
>> models.
>>
>> I would also strongly prefer to do synthetic code generation for
>> tests so that we know the answer rather than relying on comparisons
>> with BUGS.
>>
>> But all this can be in a separate project.  What we really need
>> are the models translated as a first priority.
>>
>>> 4. The simulation of the fake data should be done somehow with the fixed_param algo from rstan as Bob points out.
>>>
>>> Could we place this stuff in some git repo?
>>
>> Agreed.  Ben --- we can give you push permission if you give us your
>> GitHub handle.  For us, nothing exists that's not in GitHub.
>>
>> - Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] what do do about weights in tan_regression
messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] what do do about weights in tan_regression
messages.body_plain:
Bob:
The trouble is that weights are used in many different ways for different purposes.  When a survey respondent has a weight of 3.1, this does not mean that there were 3.1 respondents who gave these exact same respondents.  What it means is that this person represents (based on some model) 3.1 people in the population.  You can perhaps already see the problem here.  The analogy with MI is not a good one.  With MI we can see the imputations as an approximation to Bayesian inference given a poorly specified model.  With weighting there’s no implicit model at all.  Also, yes, linear regression is Bayesian even though N and x are not modeled.  The implicit assumption is separability of (N,x) and y in the posterior.  We discuss this near the beginning of the regression chapter of BDA.
A

messages.subject: Re: what do do about weights in stan_regression
messages.subject_clean: what do do about weights in stan_regression
messages.body_plain:
I think we should allow non-integer weights.  R returns an error if you give it negative weights, so we can do that too.

The only trouble is, I don’t quite know what R is doing with the weights.

Here’s an example:

> y <- 1:5
> w <- 1:5
> display(lm(y~1))
lm(formula = y ~ 1)
            coef.est coef.se <http://coef.se>
(Intercept) 3.00     0.71
---
n = 5, k = 1
residual sd = 1.58, R-Squared = 0.00
> display(lm(y~1, weight=w))
lm(formula = y ~ 1, weights = w)
            coef.est coef.se <http://coef.se>
(Intercept) 3.67     0.62
---
n = 5, k = 1
residual sd = 2.42, R-Squared = 0.00

OK, so far so good.  We gave higher weights to the big values, so beta.hat goes up.

But then check this out:

> display(lm(y~1, weight=10*w))
lm(formula = y ~ 1, weights = 10 * w)
            coef.est coef.se <http://coef.se>
(Intercept) 3.67     0.62
---
n = 5, k = 1
residual sd = 7.64, R-Squared = 0.00

I multiplied al the weights by 10, and what happened?  The coef estimate did not change (fine), but the se did not change either!  Which suggests it’s doing some sort of normalization with the weights.  Which I don’t actually want because now I don’t know what’s going on.  Also, the residual sd increased, which suggests that it’s a weight-scaled sd, not a residual sd at all.

OK, now let’s try logistic regression:

> display(glm(y~1, family=binomial(link="logit")))
glm(formula = y ~ 1, family = binomial(link = "logit"))
            coef.est coef.se <http://coef.se>
(Intercept) 0.41     0.91
---
  n = 5, k = 1
  residual deviance = 6.7, null deviance = 6.7 (difference = 0.0)
> display(glm(y~1, weight=w, family=binomial(link="logit")))
glm(formula = y ~ 1, family = binomial(link = "logit"), weights = w)
            coef.est coef.se <http://coef.se>
(Intercept) -0.41     0.53
---
  n = 5, k = 1
  residual deviance = 20.2, null deviance = 20.2 (difference = 0.0)
> display(glm(y~1, weight=10*w, family=binomial(link="logit")))
glm(formula = y ~ 1, family = binomial(link = "logit"), weights = 10 *
    w)
            coef.est coef.se <http://coef.se>
(Intercept) -0.41     0.17
---
  n = 5, k = 1
  residual deviance = 201.9, null deviance = 201.9 (difference = 0.0)

_This_ time when we multiply all weights by 10, the se of the coefficient decreases by the expected factor of sqrt(10).

So . . . it seems to me that R is not coherent in what it does with lm and glm.  (By the way, if you run glm with family=“gaussian”, you reproduce the lm results.)  Which suggests to me that we do not need to preserve compatibility with R here!

My suggestion is that we disallow negative or missing weights, and that when weights are supplied we use increment_log_prob with the specified weights.  This is clean and clear.  The only concern is that the autogenerated Stan code will now be uglier.  I suppose we’ll have to have stan_regression generate different Stan programs, depending on whether it is called with or without weights.

> On Jun 24, 2015, at 12:00 AM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> On Tuesday, June 23, 2015 at 11:07:01 PM UTC-4, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> > For now I guess we should follow Bob’s advice and use increment_log_prob() with weights, and when weights are specified in stan_regression, we spit out a warning and also print out the sum of the weights.
>
> I guess there are several situations:
> For MLE that happens to use Stan's optimization algorithm, I think it is self-evident that stan_foo() should handle the weights in the same way as foo().
> For penalized MLE, MCMC, and things like that, we could follow Bob's suggestion (presumably  disallowing negative weights), but I have a hard time coming up with any rationale for non-integer weights in a Bayesian GLM.
> For the case where glm() does "For a binomial GLM prior weights are used to give the number of trials when the response is the proportion of successes", that also makes complete sense from a Bayesian perspective (provided weight[i] * y[i] is an integer). Sometimes medical data comes this way because they don't want to individually identify the successes and failures.
> More generally, in any case where the weights are non-negative integers and represent the number of cases observed in the sample with that data, I wouldn't mind throwing an error that says, in effect, "duplicate each row i weight[i] times and try again without weights".
> Generalized Least Squares is Ordinary Least Squares on transformed data, so it doesn't seem particularly problematic from a Bayesian perspective to do a Gaussian model on the transformed data.
>
> Other opinions?
>
>
> Ben
>

messages.subject: Var Context Return Types
messages.body_plain:
In trying to refactor everything I’ve realized that the current var_context
implementation is awkward because it’s sort of in the middle of two
functionalities.  On one hand you could imagine the var_context just
returning an unstructured array of values corresponding to a variable
name, and on the other you could imagine the var_context returning
a properly formatted type.  For example, calling

Eigen::VectorXd v = context.get_vals_r(“vector_name”);

would be incredibly useful to the internal code.

But right now var_context does something in between.  It returns
a set of unstructured values but does know something about its
structure which is partially validated (namely the dims).  This then
requires that the client know what type to be expecting, which is
fine for the generator but not for user-facing code.

Is there a pattern that would allow us to implement dynamic return types?
I can imagine metaprograms that properly map a block of vector data
in the var_context into the appropriate output (instead of having a dims
vector we’d have a type class which would not only contain the dim
information but also the type information) but I don’t see how we could
get dynamic return types with a single function signature.

Or should the user have to specify the type for validation?  i.e.

template <typename T>
T var_context::get_vars_r(std::string& name) {
  if (! contains_r(name))
    throw unknown variable exception;
  if (! T == type(name) )
    throw type mismatch exception;

  return convert<T>(vals_r(name);
}

In this case, how could the types be checked for equality dynamically?

messages.subject: block-diagonal mass matrix?
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

So far we have HMC with full mass matrix or diagonal mass matrix (and the diagonal version works a lot faster, I know). But what about block-diagonal mass-matrices? Maybe these would make sense in some applications?

For example, we often have varying parameters on some unit of interest. These individual parameters which are made specific in a hierachichal model to the unit of interest will always be correlated and hence a block in the mass matrix for these parameters would make sense.

Specifically, I am thinking about patients which are described by a set of parameters - those parameters which I fit with a hierarchical model specific to a patient will end up being correlated and hence a block for the patient-level would maybe make sense?

I know, identifying this structure from the model is another story...

Best,
Sebastian

that could be combined with block-diagonal structure.

are also correlated.  And of course, if they all go in a regression,

messages.body_plain:
I agree it would be great to avoid templates wherever possible on the
client-facing code because it seems like supporting templates in C++
glue packages has proven hard in the past. For example, it was a very
late addition to Cython.

> No need for template polymorphism then.
>
> - Bob

> > On Jun 25, 2015, at 5:27 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > In trying to refactor everything I’ve realized that the current var_context
> > implementation is awkward because it’s sort of in the middle of two
> > functionalities.  On one hand you could imagine the var_context just
> > returning an unstructured array of values corresponding to a variable
> > name, and on the other you could imagine the var_context returning
> > a properly formatted type.  For example, calling
> >
> > Eigen::VectorXd v = context.get_vals_r(“vector_name”);
> >
> > would be incredibly useful to the internal code.
> >
> > But right now var_context does something in between.  It returns
> > a set of unstructured values but does know something about its
> > structure which is partially validated (namely the dims).  This then
> > requires that the client know what type to be expecting, which is

> > in the var_context into the appropriate output (instead of having a dims

> > information but also the type information) but I don’t see how we could

messages.subject: StataStan alpha-testing version online
messages.body_plain:
StataStan is the new interface to call CmdStan and get results back from inside Stata. An alpha-testing version is now online at https://github.com/stan-dev/statastan/tree/alpha-test and we want to check initially that it works all right across operating systems and versions/flavors of Stata. It's mostly been worked up in Debian and then tested in Windows V*sta, with Stata 11 and 13, IC and SE. If you're even an occasional Stata user, please try it out and give us feedback here or on GitHub or just by emailing me at rober...@live.com

There's an introductory blog post at https://robertgrantstats.wordpress.com/2015/06/26/introducing-statastan/

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Proposed Var Context Refactor
messages.body_plain:
Some comments in line.

We could also do a hangout to discuss more.

> On Jun 29, 2015, at 11:13 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Will everyone take some time to look through the proposed refractor
> on feature/refactor_io_reader_writer?  There’s a lot more work to be
> done but the basic pattern is in place and I don’t want to implement
> everything only to have the pattern change later.
>
> The biggest change is that src/stan/io/writer.hpp and src/stan/io/reader.hpp
> have been refactored into src/stan/io/transforms, with one file per
> transform.

I think that's a very good idea.

>  This not only cleans up the model code, simplifies testing, etc,
> but admits new methods in var_context,
>
> void var_context::get_unconstrained_vector(std::vector<double>& parameters,
>                                      const std::string& name,
>                                      const std::string& scope,
>                                      size_t N,
>                                      stan::io::vector_transform& transform) {
>          vector_t constr_val = vector(name, N);
>          transform.unconstrain(constr_val, parameters);
> }

I'm afraid I didn't understand the intent of this method.

* The standard convention is to make the return type non-constant args
  last in argument lists (we haven't been so good about that, but it's
  another thing I try to do and Google code urges us to do).

* What's the scope argument?  It's not used in the implementation.

* (See below --- I rethought this after writing, but want to throw it
   out there anyway.)

  Why is an unconstrain transform an argument rather than being
  built into the function named get_unconstrained_vector.  Is the idea
  that you might pass in either logit + bounds or log + location + sign?
  I'd prefer just having mulitple functions exposed to the API client
  so that the creating of the transform and getting of the unconstrained vec
  was one call:

    void get_lb_unconstrained(
      const string& name,
      double lb,
      size_t n,
      vector<double>& unconstrained_vec);

  And then a whole bunch more.  They could call the more generic
  thing above if there's a reason to have the transforms not be
  static.

> The new var_context (and its derivations) can be found in
> src/stan/interface/var_context.  Note also the structured accessors,
>
> double var_context::scalar(const std::string& name)
> vector_t var_context::vector(const std::string& name, size_t N)
> row_vector_t var_context::row_vector(const std::string& name, size_t N)
> matrix_t var_context::matrix(const std::string& name, size_t n_rows, size_t n_cols)

Right --- this is more what I was thinking.
But now I realize we're looking at

  no bound
  lower bound
  upper bound
  lower & upper bound

crossed with:

  real
  vector
  row vector
  matrix

for each function.  I'd just built those up over time in a really
awful way in the generated code itself.

OK, so now I'm not so sure about my suggestion above.  But then
I'm also not so sure on how far to go with traits to reduce the
total number of functions (which all else being equal is a good thing).
Or how to encapsulate --- do I pass the matrix readers an unconstrained
reader?

> With these changes the model code becomes substantially cleaner.
> For example, in the constructor something like
>
> context__.validate_dims("data initialization", "a", "matrix_d", context__.to_vec(5,5));
>        validate_non_negative_index("a", "5", 5);
>        validate_non_negative_index("a", "5", 5);
>        a = matrix_d(5,5);
>        vals_r__ = context__.vals_r("a");
>        pos__ = 0;
>        size_t a_k_mat_lim__ = 5;
>        for (size_t n_mat__ = 0; n_mat__ < a_k_mat_lim__; ++n_mat__) {
>            for (size_t m_mat__ = 0; m_mat__ < a_k_mat_lim__; ++m_mat__) {
>                a(m_mat__,n_mat__) = vals_r__[pos__++];
>            }
>        }
>
> stan::math::check_cov_matrix(function__,"a",a);
>
> becomes
>
> validate_non_negative_index("a", "5", 5);
> validate_non_negative_index("a", "5", 5);
> a = context__.matrix(“a”, 5, 5);
> stan::math::check_cov_matrix(function__,"a",a);

This will be awesome and very easy to change in the generator.
And thanks for working out this detail so I don't have to reason
through it myself.

> Similarly,
>
>        if (!(context__.contains_r("beta")))
>            throw std::runtime_error("variable beta missing");
>        vals_r__ = context__.vals_r("beta");
>        pos__ = 0U;
>        context__.validate_dims("initialization", "beta", "vector_d", context__.to_vec(5));
>        vector_d beta(5);
>        for (int j1__ = 0U; j1__ < 5; ++j1__)
>            beta(j1__) = vals_r__[pos__++];
>        try {
>            writer__.ordered_unconstrain(beta);
>        } catch (const std::exception& e) {
>            throw std::runtime_error(std::string("Error transforming variable beta: ") + e.what());
>        }
>
> becomes
>
> try {
>  context__.get_unconstrained_vector(params_r, “beta”, “initialization”, 5, stan::io::vector_ordered(5));
> } catch(const std::exception& e) {
>  throw std::runtime_error(e.what());
> }

* I'm missing where the assignment to the local variable is, so I think
  that should be:

     beta = context__.get_unconstrained_vector(...);

   or

     context__.get_unconstrained_vector(..., beta);

* Is the "initialization" just for error messages?  If so, we can perhaps
  try/catch around the whole block to add a location if it's helpful so
  we don't have to clutter all these up --- though I guess I'm not too bothered
  by this

* Whatever we do, we shouldn't have those char* converted to std::string
  on the fly if we can help it.  We found that to have a pretty high overhead
  in tight interfaces (I'm suring it's doing it now, but it'd be nice to
  get rid of).

* I think we can go one step further and roll the exception
  throwing into the get_unconstrained_vector operation itself

* Having to redundantly specify the 5 is a place programmers
  (like me during code gen) can make errors.

  Is there a way to make vector_ordered a simple transform that
  takes size arguments?  The issue is then what to do with transforms
  that don't require sizes?

  I can see this going by way of templates, with:

    context__.get_unconstrained_vector<vector_ordered>(params_r, "beta", 5);

  and that's implemented by calling a static function

    vector_ordered::transform(5);

  But then I'm not quite sure on how to make that more general to deal with
  all the permutations:

    context__.get_unconstrained_matrix<lower_bound>(params_r, "Sigma", 0, 5, 7);

  The lower bound of 0 needs to get to the lower_bound constraint and the 5 x 7
  dims needs to be handled by get_unconstrained_matrix.

  I'm back to thinking just blowing it all out wouldn't be such a bad idea.

> We can also change the log_prob code and move from using std::vectors in all of the model
> methods to Eigen::Vectors is desired.

Didn't that already happen?  Or are we still wrapping?  We could perhaps provide
both if we could deal with the abstraction properly --- they both give us size() and
operator[].

> It’d be nice to settle on this pattern as soon as possible so I can start the onerous task
> of implementing everything.

Agreed.  If you want help, I can implement some of it.

>  If you don’t like it then suggest an alternative — we’re already
> way behind on the refactor.  Also, I’ll be at a conference tomorrow so I won’t be online but
> I should have plenty of email access.

This should keep you busy during boring talks.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Proposed Var Context Refactor
messages.body_plain:
> I'm afraid I didn't understand the intent of this method.

It allows this,

try {
 context__.get_unconstrained_vector(params_r, “beta”, “initialization”, 5, stan::io::vector_ordered(5));
} catch(const std::exception& e) {
 throw std::runtime_error(e.what());
}

In particular, it makes partial random inits trivial.  See
src/stan/interface/var_context/random_var_context.hpp

> * The standard convention is to make the return type non-constant args
>  last in argument lists (we haven't been so good about that, but it's
>  another thing I try to do and Google code urges us to do).

We can fix order of headers and args later after the signatures
have been finalized.

> * What's the scope argument?  It's not used in the implementation.

It’s used to construct exceptions — see below about cleaning
all of that up.

> * (See below --- I rethought this after writing, but want to throw it
>   out there anyway.)
>
>  Why is an unconstrain transform an argument rather than being
>  built into the function named get_unconstrained_vector.  Is the idea
>  that you might pass in either logit + bounds or log + location + sign?
>  I'd prefer just having mulitple functions exposed to the API client
>  so that the creating of the transform and getting of the unconstrained vec
>  was one call:
>
>    void get_lb_unconstrained(
>      const string& name,
>      double lb,
>      size_t n,
>      vector<double>& unconstrained_vec);
>
>  And then a whole bunch more.  They could call the more generic
>  thing above if there's a reason to have the transforms not be
>  static.

This couples the transforms and the var_context — every time you create
a new transform it has to be reimplemented (or at least wrapped) in the
var_context.  We have way too much duplication like this is in the code
already and it makes adding new features a pain in the ass.

> OK, so now I'm not so sure about my suggestion above.  But then
> I'm also not so sure on how far to go with traits to reduce the
> total number of functions (which all else being equal is a good thing).
> Or how to encapsulate --- do I pass the matrix readers an unconstrained
> reader?

What’s a matrix reader?

> > try {
> > context__.get_unconstrained_vector(params_r, “beta”, “initialization”, 5, stan::io::vector_ordered(5));
> > } catch(const std::exception& e) {
> > throw std::runtime_error(e.what());
> > }

> * I'm missing where the assignment to the local variable is, so I think
>  that should be:
>
>     beta = context__.get_unconstrained_vector(...);
>
>   or
>
>     context__.get_unconstrained_vector(..., beta);

There is no more local variable.  get_unconstrained grabs the constrained
values, unconstrained them, and then appends the unconstrained values
to the params_r vector.

> * Is the "initialization" just for error messages?  If so, we can perhaps
>  try/catch around the whole block to add a location if it's helpful so
>  we don't have to clutter all these up --- though I guess I'm not too bothered
>  by this

We have to be careful with what throws where, but, yes, this was my thinking
and would be implemented as the refactor is implemented in earnest.

> * Whatever we do, we shouldn't have those char* converted to std::string
>  on the fly if we can help it.  We found that to have a pretty high overhead
>  in tight interfaces (I'm suring it's doing it now, but it'd be nice to
>  get rid of).

Easy fix once we finalize the signatures.

> * I think we can go one step further and roll the exception
>  throwing into the get_unconstrained_vector operation itself

As I warned above this will be tricky as the transforms call free/constrain
functions that themselves can throw exceptions.  And we have to be careful
to validate constraints but without validating them too often.

> * Having to redundantly specify the 5 is a place programmers
>  (like me during code gen) can make errors.

This is all over the current code generator.  Not sure how to simplify it.

>  Is there a way to make vector_ordered a simple transform that
>  takes size arguments?  The issue is then what to do with transforms
>  that don't require sizes?
>
>  I can see this going by way of templates, with:
>
>    context__.get_unconstrained_vector<vector_ordered>(params_r, "beta", 5);
>
>  and that's implemented by calling a static function
>
>    vector_ordered::transform(5);
>
>  But then I'm not quite sure on how to make that more general to deal with
>  all the permutations:
>
>    context__.get_unconstrained_matrix<lower_bound>(params_r, "Sigma", 0, 5, 7);
>
>  The lower bound of 0 needs to get to the lower_bound constraint and the 5 x 7
>  dims needs to be handled by get_unconstrained_matrix.
>
>  I'm back to thinking just blowing it all out wouldn't be such a bad idea.

See the current transform implementations — they’re stateful classes to store things
like bounds and sizes.  That way everything can be wrapped in a single
get_unconstrained function.  Because bounds can be dynamic I don’t think there’s
any other way.

> > We can also change the log_prob code and move from using std::vectors in all of the model
> > methods to Eigen::Vectors is desired.
>
> Didn't that already happen?  Or are we still wrapping?  We could perhaps provide
> both if we could deal with the abstraction properly --- they both give us size() and
> operator[].

Nope, they wrap.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Proposed Var Context Refactor
messages.body_plain:
I had completely confused which direction you were
going here.

Let me take a shot at documenting the intent now.  It
is a var_context method, right?

/**
 * Reads an N-vector of the specified name out of this variable
 * context and appends it to the end of the parameters vector,
 * after applying the specified transform.
 *
 * The scope variable just indicates context for constructing an
 * error message.  There will be an error if the variable in
 * this var_context is not of size N (or if the transformed value is
 * not of size N?).
 */
void var_context::get_unconstrained_vector(

    std::vector<double>& parameters,
    const std::string& name,
    const std::string& scope,
    size_t N,

    stan::io::vector_transform& transform);

As you can see, I'm still confused about specifying the sizes twice.
Is the N for the number of constrained or unconstrained values?  Same
question for the argument to transform.

This is why I find it easier if the N is from the consumer's point of view.
That is, the model wants an N-simplex, so N is the number of dimensions, which
corresponds to (N - 1) unconstrained values.  I don't then know which you
want to specify to the transform.

> On Jun 29, 2015, at 12:45 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> This couples the transforms and the var_context — every time you create
> a new transform it has to be reimplemented (or at least wrapped) in the
> var_context.  We have way too much duplication like this is in the code
> already and it makes adding new features a pain in the ass.

I wouldn't say it's so much duplication as it is composing existing functions
to hide the internals to simplify the external interfaces.  But I agree
it's a tradeoff, and as I said, I can live with the redundancy and cut-and-paste
(or cut-and-paste and resize) of sizes --- we'll just have to be very careful in
testing it all.

By "matrix reader", I just meant whatever did the same thing for matrices,
probably named "get_unconstrained_matrix".  And there, you have more parameters
to play with that have to be synchronized across the equivalent of size N and
the equivalent of the arguments to the transform that might get messed up.

> As I warned above this will be tricky as the transforms call free/constrain
> functions that themselves can throw exceptions.  And we have to be careful
> to validate constraints but without validating them too often.

I had the opposite concern --- I don't want to have to generate try/catch
any more in our model code --- it's just more redundancy that should be
rolled into the transforms (or even below if the transforms throw).  So I
think we're on the same page here.

>> Didn't that already happen?  Or are we still wrapping?  We could perhaps provide
>> both if we could deal with the abstraction properly --- they both give us size() and
>> operator[].
>
> Nope, they wrap.

Can we resize an Eigen vector?  Or do we just reallocate and copy?  If so,
we won't be able to work efficiently directly with an Eigen vector unless we
knew how big it was and kept an offset along with all the rest of this.

- Bob
